Transports. stdio for local servers started as subprocesses, and Streamable HTTP for remote servers (it replaced the earlier HTTP+SSE transport). Remote authorization is based on OAuth 2.1. The specification is still evolving, so check the current revision.

Security concerns.

  • Tool descriptions and tool results are untrusted text that enters the model’s context: a malicious or compromised server can inject instructions (“tool poisoning”).
  • A server holds real credentials; over-broad scopes and token pass-through create confused-deputy problems.
  • A local stdio server runs with the user’s privileges.
  • The host’s sandbox does not automatically cover what an MCP server does.

Mitigations: allowlist servers, pin versions, least-privilege scopes, per-tool approval for writes, and treat everything returned as data.

  • How is an MCP tool different from a function you define in the request?
  • Fifty MCP servers are connected and tool definitions fill the context. What do you do?

Two percent of your agent’s tool calls are malformed. How do you investigate and fix it?

Two percent per call is not small: over a 20-call trajectory the chance of at least one malformed call is \(1 - 0.98^{20} \approx 33\%\).

Classify the failures from logs first.

  • Invalid JSON: usually truncation (finish reason is length), or unescaped quotes and newlines inside long string arguments such as code or documents.
  • Schema-invalid: missing required field, wrong type, invented enum value.
  • Unknown tool name: hallucinated or from a stale tool list.
  • Client bug: streamed argument deltas concatenated in the wrong order or across calls.

Look for what the failures correlate with. One tool, long arguments, long context, parallel calls, a model version, streaming versus non-streaming.

Fixes, most effective first.

  1. Turn on schema-constrained (strict) tool calling if the provider offers it; this removes syntax and schema errors, except truncation.
  2. Raise the output token limit, and treat length as an error rather than parsing a partial call.
  3. Simplify the schema: flatten nesting, fewer optional fields, enums, and move large payloads out of JSON (write to a file, pass a reference).
  4. Validate before execution and return the validation error to the model for one bounded repair attempt.
  5. Fix the streaming accumulator (key deltas by call index).
  6. Tighten the description, add one example of a correct call.

Then make the malformed-call rate a tracked metric per tool and per model version, alert on it, and add the failing inputs to the regression suite so a model or prompt change that brings it back is caught.

  • Constrained decoding is on and you still see failures. What are they?
  • Why not just retry the whole request?

When would you give an agent computer or browser use instead of API tools, and how do you contain it?

Computer use means the model perceives a screen (screenshots, sometimes with a DOM or accessibility tree) and emits mouse and keyboard actions in a perceive-act loop. It is the tool of last resort: use it when the target has no API (legacy desktop software, third-party sites, UI testing).

Order of preference. A structured API tool; then browser automation over the DOM or accessibility tree (text is cheaper and more reliable to ground than pixels); then pixel-level control.

Why it is last.

  • Slow: every step is a screenshot plus a model call, so seconds per action and minutes per task.
  • Expensive: image tokens on every step.
  • Brittle: layout changes, pop-ups, loading states, mis-grounded click coordinates.
  • Hard to verify: success must be checked from the resulting state, not from the model’s claim.
  • Large attack surface: any text on any page is a potential injected instruction, and the agent may hold a logged-in session.

Containment. Run in an isolated VM or a dedicated browser profile with no ambient credentials; allowlist domains; require human confirmation for logins, purchases, sending messages and anything irreversible; cap steps and time; record the session; verify the end state with an independent check.

Evaluation. Task success on sandboxed, resettable sites or VMs, with steps and cost per task; expect high run-to-run variance, so run each task several times.

  • How do you check that a form was actually submitted?
  • What would you do about a page that tells the agent to email its cookies somewhere?

What goes into the context window of a production LLM feature, and how do you order it?

Context engineering is choosing the smallest set of high-signal tokens that makes the next output correct. The layers:

  1. Rules: role, policies, output contract. Stable and authoritative.
  2. Tool definitions.
  3. Reference material: retrieved documents, few-shot examples.
  4. State: plan, progress, known constraints, open errors.
  5. History: recent turns and tool results.
  6. The current request.

Ordering principles:

  • Stable first, volatile last. Prompt caches match on the prefix, so tools, system prompt and fixed documents go first; timestamps, user-specific data and the question go last.
  • Long documents before the question, with the instruction restated at the end. Models attend best to the start and end of long inputs (“lost in the middle”), so do not bury the key instruction or the key passage mid-context.
  • Delimit data from instructions (tags or fenced sections) and label untrusted content as data to be analysed, not obeyed.
  • Say why, not just what. A short reason for a rule generalises better than emphasis.

Few-shot examples: three to five, diverse, covering edge cases, in exactly the output format you want. For heterogeneous inputs, select examples per request by similarity. Models copy surface features of examples, so near-identical examples narrow the output.

Failure modes: contradictory instructions accumulated over time, stale retrieved content, tool outputs that swamp the window, and treating a transcript dump as state.

  • How would you test whether an instruction in the prompt is still doing anything?
  • When do few-shot examples make outputs worse?

Your agent’s context fills up on long tasks. What are the compaction strategies and what can go wrong?

Quality degrades before the hard limit: long, noisy contexts make models miss instructions and reuse stale information. So manage context continuously, not only at overflow.

Strategies, cheapest first.

  1. Bound tool output at the source: return the relevant slice, store the full output as an artefact with a pointer.
  2. Clear old tool results: keep the record that the call happened, drop the bulky payload that can be re-fetched.
  3. Summarise history into structured state: goal, user constraints, decisions and their reasons, files or entities touched, open errors, failed attempts, next steps.
  4. Externalise: write notes or plans to files or a memory store and re-read on demand.
  5. Isolate: push exploration into a sub-agent that returns only its conclusion.

What must survive verbatim. User constraints, the definition of done, unresolved errors, the reasons earlier approaches failed, and source attributions.

Costs. Summaries are lossy, and rewriting history invalidates the prompt cache from that point, so compaction trades a one-time cache miss for a smaller context. Trigger at a threshold well below the limit so the summary itself has room.

Failure modes. The agent repeats an approach whose failure was summarised away; a user constraint disappears; the summary states a guess as a fact.

How to test. Evals that interrupt a run, compact, and resume; compare task success and repeated-action rate with and without compaction.

  • How do you choose between clearing tool results and summarising?
  • What is the compaction analogue of a regression test?

Context windows now reach a million tokens. Why still build retrieval, and when would you just put everything in the prompt?

Put it all in the prompt when the corpus is small enough to fit comfortably, changes rarely, and every user may see all of it. With prompt caching the repeated prefix is cheap on later requests, there is no retrieval miss, and the model can reason across documents. This is the right first version for a knowledge base of tens to a few hundred pages.

Build retrieval when any of these holds:

  • Size: the corpus exceeds the window, or will.
  • Cost and latency: input cost and time to first token scale with prompt length on every request; at high QPS a long prompt per request dominates the bill even with caching.
  • Access control: different users may see different documents, which breaks a shared cached prefix and makes “put everything in” a leak.
  • Freshness: documents change; re-indexing a changed document is cheaper than invalidating a huge cached prompt.
  • Accuracy: irrelevant material acts as distractors, and recall of a specific fact drops as context grows.
  • Attribution: retrieval gives a natural unit for citations.

Retrieval’s weakness is that a one-shot miss is unrecoverable: if the passage is not in the top k, the model cannot answer. Global questions (“summarise the themes across all contracts”) also do badly with top-k chunks.

The middle option is agentic retrieval: give the model search and read tools and let it iterate. It recovers from misses and handles multi-hop questions, at the price of more calls and latency.

Decide from corpus size against window, update rate, QPS times tokens, permission model, and question types, and confirm with an eval rather than by argument.

  • How would you measure the distractor effect on your own data?
  • What does per-user access control do to your cache hit rate?
  • OpenAI, Product Manager, Apr 2026: How context window length affects quality, cost and latency (PracHub)
  • OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, undated: Effect of adjusting an LLM’s context window size (Aced (formerly Exponent))

How does prompt caching work, and how does it change the way you lay out a prompt?

The provider stores the model’s computed state for a prompt prefix. A later request whose prompt starts with exactly the same tokens reuses it, so those input tokens are billed at a discount and time to first token drops.

It is a prefix match. A change at any position invalidates everything after it. So the layout is: tool definitions, then system prompt, then fixed reference material, then conversation history, then the volatile part (current question, timestamps, per-request data).

Silent invalidators.

  • A timestamp, request id or user name near the top of the system prompt.
  • Non-deterministic serialisation: unsorted JSON keys, tools listed in varying order.
  • Adding or removing a tool mid-conversation.
  • Rewriting earlier history (compaction, trimming, editing a message).
  • Switching models; caches are per model.

Provider differences (check current documentation). Some cache automatically above a minimum prefix length; others need explicit cache breakpoints. Lifetimes are short, typically minutes, extended on use. Discounts vary: on Anthropic’s API reads cost about a tenth of the base input price and writes carry a premium of about 25%, so a cached prefix pays off from the second request.

Why it matters most for agents. Each step re-sends the whole history. With an append-only history, each step pays full price only for the new tokens.

Operate it. Log cached versus uncached input tokens per request, track the hit rate, and alert when it falls; a prompt edit that drops the hit rate to zero can multiply cost with no visible behaviour change.

  • You need the current date in the prompt. Where do you put it?
  • How would you inject a new operator instruction mid-conversation without losing the cache?

How do you run prompt engineering as an engineering discipline rather than trial and error?

Treat prompts, tool descriptions and model settings as code with tests.

  • Version control. Prompts live in the repository as templates, separate from the data interpolated into them. Every production trace records the prompt version and the model version.
  • Regression suite. A golden set of inputs with graders (code checks where possible, validated LLM judges otherwise) runs on every change. The pull request shows per-slice scores and the individual examples that flipped, not only the average.
  • Held-out data. Tune against a development split and confirm on a held-out split. Editing a prompt until five hand-picked examples pass is overfitting.
  • Pinned models. Use dated model snapshots, not moving aliases. A model upgrade is a change like any other: re-run the suite and expect to re-tune, because instructions written to compensate for an older model’s weaknesses can hurt a newer one.
  • Staged rollout. Shadow or canary, then A/B on online metrics.
  • Root cause before patching. When an output is wrong, find out whether it is missing context, a conflicting instruction, a retrieval miss or a tool problem. Appending “IMPORTANT: never do X” for each incident produces a long, contradictory prompt.
  • Injection surface. Keep an inventory of every place where user, document or tool text is interpolated into the prompt; each is an attack surface and needs delimiting and downstream controls.

Automated prompt optimisation (DSPy-style) fits the same frame: it needs a metric and a dataset, and its output is reviewed and tested like a human-written prompt.

  • A prompt change fixes one customer’s issue and lowers the suite score by a point. Ship?
  • How large does the golden set need to be to detect a 3-point regression?
  • OpenAI / Anthropic, Machine Learning Engineer, undated: Your approach to prompt engineering (Aced (formerly Exponent))

Walk me through a RAG system end to end, offline and online, and say where it usually breaks.

Offline (ingestion).

  1. Parse: PDFs, HTML, slides, tables, scans (OCR). Layout and table extraction quality bounds everything downstream.
  2. Chunk: split into retrievable units, keeping structure (headings, tables, code).
  3. Enrich: metadata per chunk (source, title, section path, date, version, permissions).
  4. Embed and index: a vector index plus a lexical (BM25) index.
  5. Keep fresh: incremental updates from change events, deletions, periodic reconciliation.

Online (query).

  1. Query processing: rewrite a conversational turn into a standalone query; optionally decompose or expand.
  2. Retrieve: top 50-100 candidates from dense and lexical retrieval, with metadata and permission filters applied in the retriever.
  3. Rerank: a cross-encoder or LLM reranker cuts to the best 5-10.
  4. Assemble: passages with source ids, ordered and deduplicated, within a token budget.
  5. Generate: answer only from the passages, cite ids, abstain if unsupported.
  6. Check: citation and groundedness verification before returning.

Where it breaks. Most failures are upstream of the model: a table parsed into noise, a chunk boundary that separates a number from its meaning, a query whose exact identifier dense retrieval misses, a stale version of a document outranking the current one. Fewer are generation failures: the model ignores the passage, blends in prior knowledge, or answers when it should abstain.

Changing the embedding model means re-embedding the whole corpus, so version the index.

  • Which stage would you instrument first, and with what metric?
  • How do you handle a question the corpus cannot answer?

How do you choose a chunking strategy and chunk size?

Chunk size trades retrieval precision against context. Small chunks give a focused embedding and precise matches but lose the surrounding meaning (“it increased 12%” with no subject). Large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding across several topics and spend prompt tokens on irrelevant text.

A reasonable starting point is a few hundred tokens with 10-20% overlap; treat it as a hyperparameter and tune on a retrieval eval.

Strategies:

  • Fixed size with overlap: simple baseline; splits mid-sentence and mid-table.
  • Structure-aware / recursive: split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences; keep tables, lists and code blocks whole.
  • Semantic: split where the similarity between adjacent sentences drops.
  • Small-to-big (parent-child): index small chunks for matching, return the enclosing section to the model.
  • Contextual chunks: prepend the document title and section path, or a short model-written sentence situating the chunk, before embedding. This repairs lost referents.

Choose by document type: structured manuals and code favour structure-aware splitting; transcripts and prose favour semantic or sliding windows; FAQs are one chunk per question.

Evaluate with recall@k and nDCG on labelled queries, and end-to-end answer correctness. Looking at a few chunks is not an evaluation.

Failure modes: answers that span a boundary, split tables, overlap that returns the same text twice, and chunks so short that everything matches weakly.

  • Recall@10 is fine but answers lack context. What do you change?
  • How does the embedding model’s maximum input length constrain your choice?

Why use hybrid retrieval and a reranker, and when does query rewriting help?

Hybrid. Dense retrieval matches meaning and paraphrase but is weak on exact tokens it did not learn well: product codes, error strings, rare names, new jargon. Lexical retrieval (BM25) is the opposite: exact on tokens, blind to synonyms. Their errors are complementary, so fusing them raises recall. Fuse with reciprocal rank fusion (rank-based, no score calibration needed) or a weighted sum of normalised scores.

Reranking. First-stage retrieval encodes query and document separately (a bi-encoder), which is fast but coarse. A cross-encoder reads the query and passage together and scores relevance much more accurately, at one forward pass per candidate. So retrieve 50-200 candidates cheaply and rerank to 5-10. Cost: tens to a few hundred milliseconds, depending on model size and candidate count.

Query rewriting.

  • Standalone rewrite: resolve “what about the second one?” into a self-contained query. Close to mandatory for multi-turn chat.
  • Decomposition: split a multi-hop question into sub-queries.
  • Expansion: add synonyms or generate several paraphrases and fuse the results.
  • HyDE: embed a hypothetical answer instead of the question, which moves the query closer to document space.

Rewriting costs an extra model call and can drift from the user’s intent, so keep the original query in the fusion.

Add each stage only if it moves recall@k or nDCG on a labelled set; a reranker on top of a retriever that misses the document fixes nothing.

  • How do you set the candidate depth before reranking?
  • When does dense-only retrieval beat hybrid?

Implement hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion.

RRF scores a document by its ranks across retrievers: \(\mathrm{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r} \frac{w_r}{k + \mathrm{rank}_r(d)}\), with \(k = 60\) by convention and ranks starting at 1. A document absent from a list contributes nothing for that list.

from collections import defaultdict

def rrf(rankings, k=60, weights=None):
    """rankings: list of ranked lists of doc ids, best first. Returns [(doc_id, score)]."""
    weights = weights or [1.0] * len(rankings)
    scores = defaultdict(float)
    for w, ranking in zip(weights, rankings):
        seen = set()
        for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            if doc_id in seen:                    # count each doc once per list
                continue
            seen.add(doc_id)
            scores[doc_id] += w / (k + rank)
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: (-x[1], str(x[0])))   # deterministic ties

def hybrid_search(query, bm25, embed, ann, top_k=10, depth=100, flt=None):
    lexical = bm25.search(query, depth, filter=flt)           # -> [doc_id, ...]
    dense = ann.search(embed(query), depth, filter=flt)       # -> [doc_id, ...]
    return rrf([lexical, dense])[:top_k]

Pitfalls:

  • RRF uses ranks only, so it needs no score normalisation but ignores how confident each retriever was. A weighted sum of normalised scores can do better if scores are calibrated.
  • Fuse at one granularity. If one retriever returns chunks and the other documents, map both to the same id first.
  • Retrieve deeper than top_k from each list, or fusion has nothing to add.
  • Apply permission and metadata filters inside each retriever. Filtering after fusion can leave fewer than top_k results, and for permissions it is the wrong place.
  • \(k\) damps the influence of top ranks; small \(k\) makes rank 1 dominate.
  • Tune weights and depth on a labelled set; follow with a reranker if latency allows.
  • Why is k around 60 and what happens at k = 0?
  • How would you add a third retriever that is much noisier than the other two?

Implement semantic chunking: split a document where the topic changes, with size limits.

Embed sentences, measure the cosine distance between neighbours, and cut at the largest jumps, subject to minimum and maximum chunk sizes.

import re
import numpy as np

def semantic_chunks(text, embed, max_tokens=400, min_tokens=80, pct=90,
                    n_tokens=lambda s: len(s.split())):
    sents = [s.strip() for s in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text) if s.strip()]
    if len(sents) < 2:
        return sents
    E = np.asarray(embed(sents), dtype=np.float32)                  # (n, d)
    E /= np.linalg.norm(E, axis=1, keepdims=True) + 1e-12
    dist = 1.0 - np.sum(E[:-1] * E[1:], axis=1)                     # (n-1,) neighbour distance
    thresh = np.percentile(dist, pct)                               # cut at the largest jumps
    chunks, cur, cur_len = [], [sents[0]], n_tokens(sents[0])
    for i in range(1, len(sents)):
        n = n_tokens(sents[i])
        topic_shift = dist[i - 1] > thresh and cur_len >= min_tokens
        if topic_shift or cur_len + n > max_tokens:
            chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
            cur, cur_len = [], 0
        cur.append(sents[i])
        cur_len += n
    chunks.append(" ".join(cur))
    return chunks

Pitfalls:

  • Single-sentence embeddings are noisy. Embedding a sliding window of two or three sentences around each position gives steadier boundaries.
  • The percentile threshold is relative to the document, so a single-topic document is still cut at its top 10% of jumps; the minimum size limits the damage.
  • A single sentence longer than max_tokens still needs a hard split.
  • The regex splitter breaks on abbreviations, decimals, code and tables. Split on structure (headings, tables, code blocks) first and apply this within sections.
  • Count tokens with the embedding model’s tokenizer, not whitespace.
  • Ingestion cost is one embedding per sentence.
  • Semantic chunking does not always beat structure-aware fixed-size chunking. Compare recall@k on labelled queries before adopting it.
  • How would you add overlap or parent-child retrieval to this?
  • What is the time complexity, and where is the cost in practice?

Users report that your RAG assistant gives confidently wrong answers. How do you find the cause and fix it?

Take a sample of wrong answers with their traces and assign each to the first stage that failed:

  1. Not in the index: the document was never ingested, was parsed badly (tables, scans), or is stale.
  2. Indexed but not retrieved: not in the top k. Vocabulary mismatch, an exact identifier dense retrieval missed, a bad chunk boundary, an over-restrictive filter.
  3. Retrieved but not in the prompt: dropped by the reranker or the token budget.
  4. In the prompt but answered wrongly: the model ignored it, blended in prior knowledge, or picked one of two conflicting or outdated passages.
  5. Unanswerable: the corpus has no answer and the model produced one anyway.

The distribution across buckets tells you where to work. Prompt edits only help buckets 4 and 5.

Fixes by bucket: better parsing and freshness monitoring (1); hybrid retrieval, query rewriting, chunking changes (2); deeper candidates, reranker tuning, larger budget (3); instructions to answer only from sources, recency and authority metadata, deduplication of versions (4); explicit abstention plus an answerability check (5).

For the “confidently” part:

  • Require a citation per claim and verify after generation that each cited passage supports its claim (entailment model or LLM judge); block or flag unsupported claims.
  • Abstain when retrieval scores are low or passages disagree.
  • Show sources to the user.

Then keep it fixed: put the failures into the regression set, and track retrieval recall and groundedness on sampled production traffic.

  • Two retrieved documents contradict each other. What should the system do?
  • How do you measure abstention quality without making the system refuse everything?

Design enterprise RAG over documents with access controls (SharePoint, Drive, Confluence, Slack) for a company with tens of thousands of employees.

Requirements to pin down. Sources and volume, freshness target for content and for permission changes, the non-negotiable (a user never sees content they cannot open at source), citations, audit, tenancy and data residency.

Ingestion. One connector per source with incremental sync (change feeds or webhooks) and a periodic full reconcile to catch missed events and deletions. Each document is stored with its ACL: users, groups, inheritance and link-sharing rules. Source principals are mapped to one company identity; group membership is synced separately because it changes without the document changing.

Enforcing permissions. Filter at retrieval, before anything reaches the model. Content the user may not see must never enter the context window; a model cannot be trusted to withhold what it has read.

  • Index-time ACLs: store allowed principals on each chunk and filter by the user’s expanded principal set. Fast, but stale until the next sync.
  • Query-time check: confirm the top results against the source system. Always current, but slower.
  • Use both: filter in the index, then verify the final few results at source.

Revocation latency is a stated SLO. Response caches and semantic caches are keyed by permission scope or disabled.

Retrieval and generation. Structure-aware chunking with title and path context; hybrid retrieval with filter-aware ANN, falling back to exact search when a user’s permitted set is small; reranking; generation with citations that link to the source, which re-checks access.

Security. Documents are untrusted input (indirect injection), so the answering model gets no write tools. Per-tenant isolation. Audit log of who queried and which documents were retrieved. PII handling and retention.

Evaluation. Per-source retrieval sets; a permission test suite with canary documents that specific test users must never retrieve, run continuously; groundedness and citation accuracy; freshness lag dashboards.

Scale risks. Group fan-out for users in thousands of groups, very selective filters degrading ANN recall, and re-embedding the corpus on a model change.

  • A user is removed from a group. Walk me through what must happen and how fast.
  • Why is filtering the generated answer not sufficient?
  • How would you test for a permission leak before launch?

How do you evaluate a RAG system? Be specific about retrieval versus generation.

Evaluate the stages separately, then end to end, because an end-to-end score cannot tell you which stage to fix.

Retrieval. Labelled pairs of query and relevant chunk or document ids.

  • recall@k: is the needed passage among the k passed on? This caps answer quality.
  • MRR or nDCG@k: is it ranked high enough to survive truncation?
  • Report by query type (lookup, multi-hop, identifier, conversational).

Generation, given the retrieved context.

  • Faithfulness / groundedness: is every claim supported by the provided passages?
  • Answer correctness against a reference answer.
  • Citation precision and recall: do citations support the claims, and are claims cited?
  • Abstention: on unanswerable questions, does it decline; on answerable ones, does it not?

Diagnostic matrix. Cross retrieval hit or miss with answer right or wrong. A hit with a wrong answer is a generation problem; a miss with a right answer means the model used prior knowledge, which is a risk; a miss with a wrong answer is a retrieval problem.

Building the set. Sample real queries and have experts label; include unanswerable, multi-hop and ambiguous queries. Synthetic questions generated from chunks are useful for volume but are lexically close to their source and overstate retrieval quality.

Graders. Retrieval metrics are computed in code. Faithfulness and correctness usually need an LLM judge, validated against human labels before it is trusted.

Online. Citation click-through, reformulation rate, thumbs, escalation to a human, and sampled traces scored by the same graders.

  • Your labelled set only marks one relevant chunk per query but several exist. What happens to your metrics?
  • How would you get retrieval labels cheaply?

Explain HNSW, IVF and product quantization, and the recall-latency-memory trade-off each one exposes.

Exact nearest-neighbour search is \(O(Nd)\) per query. Below roughly \(10^5\) vectors that is a few milliseconds and brute force is the right answer. Beyond that, approximate indexes trade recall for speed and memory.

HNSW (graph). A multi-layer proximity graph; search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily descends. Parameters: M (links per node, typically 16-64), efConstruction (build quality), efSearch (query-time beam: higher means better recall and slower). High recall at low latency, roughly logarithmic query scaling in practice. Costs: full vectors plus links in RAM, slow builds, deletes handled by tombstones.

IVF (partitioning). k-means splits the space into nlist cells (on the order of \(\sqrt{N}\)); a query scans the nprobe closest cells. nprobe is the recall-latency knob. Less memory overhead than a graph, needs training, and degrades when the data drifts from the trained centroids.

Product quantization (compression). Split each vector into \(m\) sub-vectors and replace each with the id of its nearest of 256 centroids: \(m\) bytes per vector. A 768-dimension float32 vector is 3,072 bytes; with \(m = 96\) it is 96 bytes, 32 times smaller. Distances come from lookup tables. It is lossy, so re-score the top candidates with full vectors.

Typical combinations. HNSW when the data fits in RAM; IVF-PQ at the billion scale; disk-based graphs (DiskANN-style) when RAM is the constraint. Scalar or binary quantization with re-scoring is a simpler alternative to PQ.

Always measure. Compute recall@k against exact search on a query sample and plot it against latency; ANN recall is a property of your data and parameters, not of the library.

  • How much RAM do 100 million 1,024-dimension vectors need in HNSW, roughly?
  • What happens to an IVF index as new data arrives over months?

How does metadata filtering interact with ANN search, and when is pgvector enough versus a dedicated vector database?

Filtering. Three approaches:

  • Post-filter: run ANN, then drop non-matching results. With a selective filter (1% of rows match) a top-100 search returns about one usable result.
  • Pre-filter: select matching rows, then search exactly within them. Exact and cheap when the subset is small, linear in subset size when it is not.
  • Filter-aware index traversal: skip non-matching nodes during graph search. Good at moderate selectivity; at very low selectivity the graph of matching nodes is disconnected and recall collapses unless the engine falls back to brute force.

Good engines choose by estimated selectivity. If the filter is always a tenant id, use a partition or namespace per tenant instead of a filter.

pgvector is enough when the corpus is in the millions to low tens of millions of vectors, the index fits in memory, QPS is moderate, and you benefit from one system: joins with relational data, transactions, row-level security for permissions, existing backups and operations. These thresholds are rules of thumb and depend on dimension and hardware. Filtered ANN behaviour in pgvector is version-dependent, so test it with your real filters.

A dedicated store earns its place at hundreds of millions of vectors or more, with strict p99 latency at high QPS, heavy filtered or hybrid search, many tenants, or a need for built-in quantization, disk-based indexes and sharding.

Either way, plan for the operational events: a new embedding model means re-embedding everything and a dual-index migration; shorter dimensions (Matryoshka-style embeddings) and quantization cut memory at some recall cost.

  • Your filter matches 0.1% of rows. Which strategy and why?
  • How would you migrate to a new embedding model with no downtime?

How would you design memory for an agent that works with the same user across many sessions?

Separate three things:

  • Working context: what is in the window now.
  • Session state: the conversation, plan, scratchpad and checkpoints for one task.
  • Long-term memory: what persists across sessions. Useful sub-types are semantic (facts and preferences), episodic (what happened in past sessions) and procedural (instructions and learned ways of working).

Write path. Decide who writes (the agent through an explicit tool, or a background extraction job after the session), what is written (distilled statements with a timestamp and provenance, not raw transcripts), and how conflicts resolve (a new fact supersedes or updates the old one rather than accumulating). Add expiry for things that go stale.

Read path. A small, always-loaded profile for things that matter every time; everything else retrieved on demand by search, or kept as files the agent lists and reads. Always-loaded memory costs tokens on every request and can break prompt caching if it changes often.

Failure modes.

  • Stale or wrong memory: an error written once is replayed forever. Keep provenance, let the agent verify against the current state, and prefer current observations over memory.
  • Poisoning: injected content written to memory persists across sessions and survives the end of the attack. Do not write memory from untrusted content without review.
  • Bloat: retrieval returns marginally relevant memories that distract.
  • Privacy: scope strictly by user and tenant; let users inspect and delete.

Evaluate with multi-session tasks where the answer depends on an earlier session, and measure both recall of needed memories and the rate of wrong-memory use.

Start simple: a structured profile plus notes files beats a vector store until volume demands one.

  • The user says “I moved to Berlin” and memory says Paris. What happens on write and on read?
  • When is memory better implemented as fine-tuning? When is it worse?

What is prompt injection, what is indirect prompt injection, and why can you not fix it with a better system prompt?

A language model receives instructions and data in one token stream and has no reliable way to tell them apart. Prompt injection exploits this.

  • Direct injection: the user writes text that overrides the application’s instructions (“ignore the above and…”). A jailbreak is the related attack on the model’s own safety policy rather than the application’s instructions.
  • Indirect injection: the instructions are planted in content the system reads on the user’s behalf: a web page, email, document, code comment, tool result or tool description. The user is the victim, not the attacker.

A stronger system prompt or delimiters around untrusted text lowers the success rate but does not make it zero, and an attacker can retry. So assume some injections succeed and limit what a successful one can do.

The dangerous combination is an agent that has all three of: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to send data out (web requests, email, rendering a URL or image). Remove one and exfiltration is blocked.

Defence in depth:

  • Least-privilege tools; read-only where possible.
  • Human approval for consequential or outbound actions.
  • Egress control: allowlisted domains, no auto-rendering of model-produced links or images.
  • Isolation: a quarantined model reads untrusted content and returns constrained data to a privileged one that never sees the raw text.
  • Taint tracking: once untrusted content is in context, restrict the tools available.
  • Injection classifiers on inputs and tool results, as one layer.
  • Logging and a red-team suite that measures attack success rate.
  • Your agent summarises a web page and can send email. What is the attack and what do you remove?
  • Why does markdown image rendering matter?
  • Anthropic, Product Manager, Apr 2026: Dual-use requests, jailbreaks and layered defences (PracHub)

Design the guardrails for an LLM assistant that answers from company data and can take actions. What are the layers and how do you know they work?

No single filter is sufficient; each layer covers failures the others miss.

Layer Controls Catches
Input abuse and rate limits, moderation classifier, PII detection, injection classifier abusive or policy-violating requests, bulk probing
Model system policy, a model version with tested refusal behaviour most ordinary misuse
Data and tool boundary permission-filtered retrieval, tool allowlists, argument validation, sandbox, approval for writes injection consequences, data leaks, wrong actions
Output schema validation, groundedness check against sources, PII and secret scan, moderation hallucinated claims, leaked data, harmful text
System audit log, monitoring, kill switch, incident process what slipped through

Hallucination control sits mainly at the output and data layers: answer only from retrieved sources with citations, abstain when support is missing, verify claims against their cited passages, choose from enumerated values instead of free text, and compute numbers in code.

PII. Redact in logs and traces by default, minimise what is sent to the model, and respect retention and residency terms.

Latency and UX trade-offs. Run input checks in parallel with generation and cancel on a hit. Output checks conflict with streaming: check per sentence or buffer, or accept a delayed first token on sensitive routes. Every block is a possible false positive, and over-blocking drives users away.

Knowing they work.

  • A red-team suite per threat (injection, jailbreak, exfiltration, policy violations) reporting attack success rate, re-run on every model, prompt or tool change.
  • A benign set to measure the false positive rate of each filter.
  • Online: block rate, user override or appeal rate, sampled human review of both blocked and allowed traffic.
  • Test the code-level controls directly: can the tool layer be made to act outside permissions regardless of what the model says?

The principle: prompts and classifiers reduce frequency; permissions, validation and approvals in code bound the damage.

  • Which layer would you cut first under a latency budget, and what risk do you accept?
  • How do you run an output check on a streamed answer?

How do you get reliable structured output from an LLM? What do JSON mode and schema-constrained decoding guarantee, and what do they not?

Three levels of guarantee:

  1. Prompt only (“reply in JSON with these fields”). Works most of the time; failures include prose around the JSON, trailing commas, missing fields.
  2. JSON mode. The output is syntactically valid JSON, with no guarantee about fields or types.
  3. Schema-constrained decoding (structured outputs, strict tool calling). The schema is compiled to a grammar, and at each step tokens that would violate it are masked. Output that completes always parses and matches the schema.

What constrained decoding does not guarantee:

  • Completion. Hitting the output token limit leaves truncated JSON; check the finish reason.
  • Correct values. A date field holds a valid date, not necessarily the right one.
  • Full JSON Schema. Providers support a subset (limits on recursion, numeric and string constraints, optional fields); check the documentation.
  • No refusal. The model may still decline.

Schema design matters as much as the mechanism:

  • Generation is left to right, so put reasoning or evidence fields before the verdict; forcing the answer first removes the model’s chance to think.
  • Allow null or “unknown” so the model is not forced to invent a value.
  • Use enums for categories; keep nesting shallow; describe each field.
  • For extraction, ask for the supporting quote alongside the value so it can be verified.

Then validate anyway (types with Pydantic or JSON Schema, plus business rules such as totals that must add up), and retry with the validation error on failure.

  • Why can constraining the output format reduce answer quality?
  • How would you extract fields from a scanned invoice and know which ones to trust?

Write a retry-with-validation wrapper for structured output from an LLM.

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError

def extract_json(text: str) -> str:
    start, end = text.find("{"), text.rfind("}")
    if start == -1 or end <= start:
        raise ValueError("no JSON object found in output")
    return text[start:end + 1]

def structured_call(llm, messages, schema: type[BaseModel], max_attempts=3, check=None):
    """llm(messages) -> str. Returns a validated `schema` instance or raises."""
    msgs, last_err = list(messages), None
    for attempt in range(1, max_attempts + 1):
        raw = llm(msgs)
        try:
            obj = schema.model_validate_json(extract_json(raw))
            if check is not None:
                check(obj)                       # business rules; raises ValueError
            return obj
        except (ValidationError, ValueError) as e:
            last_err = e
            msgs = list(messages) + [            # keep only the latest failed attempt
                {"role": "assistant", "content": raw},
                {"role": "user", "content":
                    f"That output was invalid:\n{e}\n"
                    "Return only a corrected JSON object that matches the schema."},
            ]
    raise RuntimeError(f"no valid output after {max_attempts} attempts: {last_err}")

Pitfalls an interviewer checks:

  • Bounded attempts. Each retry is a full paid call; two or three is the usual cap.
  • Feed back the specific error, not “try again”. The validator’s message tells the model which field to fix.
  • Do not accumulate every failed attempt in the history; it grows cost and anchors the model on its mistakes.
  • Separate transport errors (429, 5xx, timeouts) from validation errors; they need backoff, not a repair prompt.
  • Semantic checks belong in check: cross-field consistency, values present in the source text.
  • No side effects before validation succeeds.
  • Log the attempt count. A rising retry rate is an early signal of a prompt or model regression.
  • With schema-constrained decoding the wrapper is still needed for truncation, refusals and business rules.

Extensions: escalate to a stronger model on the last attempt; return a typed failure instead of raising so the caller can route to human review.

  • How would you handle a response truncated by the token limit?
  • What would you alert on in production?

Design a real-time voice agent. Where does the latency go, and how do you handle turn-taking and interruptions?

Pipeline. The cascaded design is voice activity and turn detection, streaming speech recognition, the LLM, then streaming text-to-speech. The alternative is a speech-to-speech model that consumes and emits audio directly.

Latency budget. People expect a reply within a few hundred milliseconds of finishing; beyond about a second the conversation feels broken. Typical contributions (approximate, system-dependent): end-of-turn detection 200-500 ms, final transcript 100-300 ms with streaming ASR, LLM time to first token 200-500 ms, TTS time to first audio 100-300 ms, plus network. What matters is time to first audio, not total generation time.

Reducing it. Stream every stage; start TTS on the first clause rather than the full reply; use a fast model and a short, cached prompt; co-locate services; replace a fixed silence timeout with a turn-detection model that uses what was said; speak a short acknowledgement before slow tool calls.

Turn-taking and barge-in. When the user starts speaking during playback: stop audio immediately, cancel the in-flight LLM and TTS, and truncate the stored assistant turn to what was actually spoken (this needs TTS timing information), otherwise the model believes it said things the user never heard. Echo cancellation stops the agent from interrupting itself. Short back-channels (“mm-hm”) should not count as interruptions.

Cascaded versus speech-to-speech. Cascaded gives text at every stage, so guardrails, tool calling, logging and model choice are straightforward, but it loses prosody and adds latency. Speech-to-speech is faster and more natural, and harder to inspect and control.

Evaluation. p50 and p95 voice-to-voice latency, word error rate on names, numbers and domain terms, interruption handling, task completion, and escalation rate.

  • The user gives a 16-digit number. What goes wrong and how do you make it robust?
  • How would you test barge-in automatically?

What determines the cost and latency of an LLM feature, and which levers do you pull first?

Cost per request is \(\text{uncached input} \times p_{in} + \text{cached input} \times p_{cache} + \text{output} \times p_{out}\). Output tokens (including reasoning tokens) are priced several times higher than input tokens on most APIs. An agent multiplies this by the number of steps, and each step re-sends the history.

Latency is roughly time to first token plus output tokens divided by generation speed. Time to first token grows with queueing and with uncached prompt length; total latency is dominated by output length.

Levers, in the order I would try them:

  1. Prompt caching: stable prefix, check the hit rate. No quality cost.
  2. Trim input: fewer and shorter retrieved passages, bounded tool outputs, compaction.
  3. Trim output: concise formats, no restating of the input, appropriate token limit, lower reasoning effort where it does not change results.
  4. Smaller model for easy steps (routing, extraction), kept honest by an eval.
  5. Batch API for offline work: asynchronous, typically about half price.
  6. Response caching for repeated queries: exact-match is safe; semantic caching risks wrong hits, staleness and leaking across users.
  7. Parallelise independent calls; stream to improve perceived latency (it does not shorten total time).

Measure cost per completed task, not per call. A cheaper model that needs more steps or more retries can cost more per task. Track tokens in and out, cached fraction, steps per task and latency percentiles per route.

  • Streaming is on and users still complain it is slow. What do you look at?
  • When is a semantic cache a bad idea?
  • Google, Software Engineer, Jan 2026: Choose between fast and cheap model options (PracHub)

Design model routing for an LLM product. When does a router or a cascade save money, and when does it backfire?

Two designs.

  • Router: a cheap classifier (or small LLM) predicts difficulty or intent and picks a model up front. One model call per request.
  • Cascade: call the small model first, and escalate to the large one when a check fails (schema or business validation, a verifier, low self-consistency, a learned confidence score).

Economics. With escalation rate \(e\), expected cascade cost is \(c_s + e \cdot c_l\) against \(c_l\) for always-large. It saves money only if \(c_s + e \cdot c_l < c_l\), that is \(e < 1 - c_s / c_l\), and the escalated requests pay both latencies. A router avoids the double call but its mistakes are silent: a hard query sent to the small model simply gets a worse answer.

How to set it up. Label a traffic sample with both models’ outputs and quality grades. Sweep the threshold and plot quality against cost; choose the operating point, and check quality per slice, not only on average, because routing errors concentrate in the hard tail that matters most.

Where it backfires.

  • LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; prefer external checks.
  • Two models means two prompts, two eval suites and two cache namespaces.
  • A provider upgrade to either model shifts the optimal threshold.
  • On multi-step agent tasks, a weaker model that takes more steps can cost more per task.

Alternatives to test first. The large model at lower reasoning effort; prompt caching; a fine-tuned or distilled small model for one narrow, high-volume task with a fallback to the large model on validation failure.

Monitor the route mix, escalation rate, per-route quality and cost per completed task.

  • How would you train the router, and what is its label?
  • The escalation rate doubles overnight. What happened?

Your LLM bill tripled the week after a prompt change, with flat traffic. How do you find the cause?

Decompose spend from usage logs, before and after, per route and model:

\[ \text{cost} = \text{tasks} \times \text{calls per task} \times (\text{uncached in} \cdot p_{in} + \text{cached in} \cdot p_{cache} + \text{out} \cdot p_{out}) \]

Then check each factor.

  1. Cache hit rate collapsed. The most likely cause of a step change with a small edit: the change put something dynamic (date, user name, request id) near the top of the prompt, or reordered tools, so every request misses the cache. Compare cached-token fractions; diff the rendered prompt of two consecutive requests.
  2. Input grew. New examples or documents in the prompt, multiplied by every step of every agent run.
  3. Output grew. The new instruction elicits longer answers, more reasoning tokens, or restated context.
  4. More calls per task. The change causes more tool calls, validation failures and retries, or loops. Compare the steps-per-task distribution and the retry rate.
  5. Model mix changed. A routing or fallback rule now sends more traffic to the expensive model.
  6. Not the prompt at all. A retry storm from rate limits, a batch job, or a new caller, coinciding with the change.

Fix the specific cause, then prevent recurrence: report tokens, cache hit rate, steps and cost per task in the regression suite next to quality, alert on cost per task, and set budget caps per run.

  • How would you detect a cache-breaking change in CI?
  • Quality improved with the new prompt. How do you decide whether to keep it?

What does a production-grade client for a hosted model API need to handle?

  • Rate limits. Providers limit requests and tokens per minute, often separately for input and output. Handle 429 with the retry-after header; add a client-side token bucket and a queue with backpressure so bursts wait instead of failing; give interactive traffic priority over batch.
  • Retries. Exponential backoff with jitter for 429, 5xx, timeouts and overload errors, with a cap on attempts and total time. Do not retry 4xx validation errors. A retried request may be billed twice and returns a different sample.
  • Timeouts and streaming. Long generations need streaming to avoid idle-connection timeouts. Handle errors that arrive mid-stream and decide what to do with partial output.
  • Finish reasons. Check why generation stopped before using the output: natural end, token limit (truncated), tool call, or refusal or content filter.
  • Fallbacks. A secondary model, region or provider behind a circuit breaker. Prompts and tool-call behaviour are not portable across models, so the fallback path needs its own prompt tuning and its own eval results.
  • Capacity. Know your quota against peak tokens per minute; consider provisioned throughput for latency-sensitive paths; hedge requests only where tail latency justifies the cost.
  • Observability. Log request id, model version, token counts including cached tokens, latency, finish reason and retries for every call.
  • Data terms. Retention, training use, residency, and what may be sent at all.
  • Versioning. Pin dated model versions and track deprecation dates.
  • You are at the token-per-minute limit at peak. What are your options?
  • What can go wrong when failing over to another provider mid-conversation?

LLM outputs are non-deterministic and the models behind an API change. How do you build a reliable system on that?

Where the variance comes from. Sampling (temperature, top-p). Even at temperature 0, outputs can differ between calls: floating-point results depend on batching and hardware, requests land on different replicas, and providers update serving stacks. Seed parameters are best effort. Some reasoning models do not expose sampling parameters at all.

Consequences for testing.

  • Assert properties, not exact strings: schema validity, required facts present, a grader’s verdict.
  • Run each eval case several times and report a pass rate with a confidence interval; a case that passes four times in five is a finding in itself.
  • Use record-and-replay of model responses for unit tests of the surrounding code.

Consequences for design.

  • Put anything that must be exact in code: arithmetic, lookups, permission checks.
  • Validate outputs and retry within bounds; make downstream actions idempotent.
  • Use multiple samples with voting only where the accuracy gain justifies the cost.

Model changes.

  • Pin dated snapshots; moving aliases change behaviour without a deploy on your side.
  • Snapshots are deprecated on a schedule, so migration is recurring work. Keep an eval suite that re-qualifies a new model, and expect to re-tune prompts: instructions that compensated for the old model can hurt the new one.
  • Roll out with shadow traffic or a canary, comparing quality, latency and cost.
  • Keep periodic canary prompts in production to detect upstream drift.

The goal is system-level reliability from an unreliable component, the same way distributed systems treat networks.

  • A test passes locally and fails in CI one time in ten. What do you do?
  • How do you decide the number of trials per eval case?

A finance team wants to automate invoice processing into their ERP with an LLM. How do you design the integration?

Map the process first. Receive, extract fields, match to purchase order, validate, approve, post to the ERP, handle exceptions. Use the model where judgment or unstructured input is involved (reading the document, classifying exceptions, drafting a query to the vendor). Keep matching rules, tolerances, approval limits and posting in code.

Architecture. An event (new email or upload) starts a durable workflow. Each model step returns schema-constrained output with supporting quotes; code validates it (totals add up, vendor exists, PO matches within tolerance). Passing items post through the ERP API; failing or low-confidence items go to a review queue with the evidence shown.

Auth and permissions. The workflow, not the model, holds credentials. Use delegated user tokens (OAuth, least scopes) when acting for a person, or a service account with narrowly scoped rights for back-office automation. The ERP still enforces its own authorisation; the model never sees secrets.

Idempotency. Every write carries a key derived from the business object (invoice id plus action), with a dedupe check, so retries and replays cannot double-post. Multi-step updates need compensation steps.

Audit. Record for each item: inputs, extracted values and quotes, model and prompt versions, validation results, who approved, and what was written. Auditors must be able to reconstruct why an invoice was paid.

Human review. Thresholds on confidence and amount; reviewer corrections are captured as labelled data for evals and prompt improvement.

Integration realities. API rate limits, pagination, schema changes, duplicate documents, and documents in formats the parser has not seen.

Rollout and metrics. Shadow mode against human decisions, then auto-post the high-confidence segment. Track straight-through rate, error rate from sampled audits, cycle time and cost per invoice.

  • How do you set the confidence threshold for auto-posting?
  • The ERP API times out after you send a post request. What happens next?

A customer says “we want an AI agent for our operations team”. How do you scope the engagement?

What the interviewer is testing. Whether you can turn a vague ask into a deliverable with a measurable outcome, push back constructively, and avoid building a demo nobody uses.

Structure of a strong answer.

  1. Find the workflow, not the technology. Ask who does what today, how often, how long it takes, where errors and delays are, and what a mistake costs. Watch someone do the task if possible.
  2. Pick one narrow, high-volume, measurable workflow where errors are detectable and recoverable. Decline the “do everything” agent for the first phase and say why.
  3. Define success with the customer. A baseline, a target metric (handle time, error rate, throughput), and acceptance criteria on a test set they help label. Agree who signs off.
  4. Check feasibility early. Data access, APIs and permissions, security and compliance review, the human fallback path, and who owns the system after hand-off.
  5. Plan in thin slices. A working end-to-end version on real data in the first weeks, then widen. Write down what is out of scope.
  6. Communicate in their terms. Risks, cost per task and expected accuracy with examples of failures, not architecture diagrams.

Mistakes that sink the answer. Starting with model or framework choices; accepting the customer’s proposed solution without understanding the problem; no baseline, so value cannot be shown; promising accuracy before seeing data; ignoring the people whose work changes; treating security review as a late step.

  • The executive sponsor wants full autonomy on day one. What do you say?
  • How do you handle a request you believe will not work?

Your demo impressed the customer’s executives. What stands between that demo and production, and how will you prove the system delivers value?

A demo shows that the system can work on chosen inputs. Production requires that it works on their inputs, inside their systems, with known failure behaviour.

The gaps.

  • Distribution. Real inputs are messier than demo inputs. Build an eval set from their data, with their experts defining what correct means, and report results by slice. This is usually the largest piece of work and the one that reveals whether the project is viable.
  • Integration. Their identity provider, permissions, data sources, rate limits and network constraints.
  • Reliability. Retries, timeouts, idempotent writes, a fallback path to a human, and defined behaviour when the model is unavailable or wrong.
  • Security and compliance. Data residency, retention, PII handling, vendor review, audit logs. Start this early; it sets the timeline.
  • Cost and latency at their volume, not at demo volume.
  • Operations. Monitoring, alerting, a feedback channel, a process for prompt and model updates, and a named owner after hand-off.
  • Adoption. Training, changes to how people work, and trust built through visible sources and easy correction.

Proving value.

  1. Agree the primary metric and measure the baseline before launch.
  2. Pilot with a comparison: randomised by user or team if possible; otherwise a staggered rollout, with before-and-after as the weakest option because other things change too.
  3. Track adoption and acceptance: usage, how often outputs are accepted, edited or overridden. A tool that is not used delivers nothing.
  4. Report cost per task next to the outcome metric, and audit a sample for errors the metric does not capture.

Risks to name. The last 20% of cases taking most of the effort, undefined success criteria, scope growth, and a pilot group that is not representative.

  • The pilot shows no improvement in handle time but users like it. What do you conclude?
  • Which gap would you close first if you had two weeks?

You have just joined a team shipping an LLM feature with no evaluation at all. How do you build one from zero?

  1. Define the task and what good means. Write success criteria with the people who own the product: what a correct output is, what is unacceptable, and what decision the eval must support (ship this prompt, pick this model).
  2. Collect 50-200 real inputs. From logs, support tickets or subject experts. Stratify by intent or slice, and include known failures, edge cases and inputs where the right behaviour is to refuse or ask.
  3. Read outputs before writing graders. Run the current system, read 50-100 outputs, and note what goes wrong. The failure modes you find determine what to grade.
  4. Choose graders per criterion. Code checks where the criterion is objective (schema, exact answer, tests pass); an LLM judge with a narrow rubric where it is not; human labels to calibrate the judge. Each example carries a reference answer or the rubric.
  5. Baseline and uncertainty. Record the score with a confidence interval. At 80% accuracy, 100 examples give about ±8 points at 95% confidence and 1,000 give about ±2.5, so a small set only detects large differences.
  6. Version and split. Version the dataset, graders and prompts together. Keep a held-out portion that is not used while iterating on the prompt.
  7. Wire it in. Run on every change; show per-slice scores and the examples that flipped.
  8. Grow it. Each production failure becomes a test case; refresh from current traffic.

Common mistakes: starting with generic metrics (“helpfulness 1-5”) before looking at data, an unvalidated judge, and a set made only of easy synthetic cases.

  • How do you get reference answers when experts disagree?
  • What tells you the eval set has become too easy?

What kinds of graders are there for LLM outputs, and when do you use each?

Grader Use when Strength Weakness
Exact or normalised match one correct answer (classification, multiple choice, extraction) free, deterministic brittle to formatting; useless for open text
Programmatic check the property is verifiable in code: schema valid, tests pass, SQL returns the right rows, number within tolerance, required citation present objective, cheap, fast covers only what can be coded
Reference-based similarity a reference answer exists and wording may vary cheap weak correlation with quality for open-ended text
LLM as judge subjective or semantic criteria: faithfulness, relevance, tone, rubric adherence scales, handles open text biased and noisy; must be validated against humans; costs money
Human review ground truth for new criteria, calibrating judges, high-stakes samples most trusted slow, expensive, inconsistent without guidelines

Order of preference: code first, then a validated judge, then humans for calibration and for what neither can assess.

Practical rules:

  • Grade one criterion per grader. “Overall quality 1-10” is hard to act on and hard to validate.
  • Prefer checking the outcome (does the code run, is the row in the database) over judging the text that describes it.
  • Treat graders as code: version them, test them on known-good and known-bad outputs, and measure their error rate.
  • Combine: a programmatic gate for hard requirements plus a judge for quality.
  • Give a criterion people usually send to an LLM judge that code could check.
  • How do you test a grader?

When is an LLM judge trustworthy? How do you validate one and what biases do you look for?

A judge is a classifier and is trusted only as far as it has been measured.

Validation.

  • Label 100-300 outputs by humans, ideally two per item, on the same rubric.
  • Report judge-human agreement (Cohen’s \(\kappa\) for categories, rank correlation for scores) next to human-human agreement, which is the ceiling.
  • Look at the confusion matrix: a judge that passes everything has high agreement when most outputs are good, and no power to detect regressions.
  • Hold out part of the labelled set from rubric tuning.

Known biases.

  • Position: in pairwise comparison, a preference for the first or second answer. Run both orders and count only consistent verdicts.
  • Verbosity: longer answers score higher.
  • Self-preference: judges tend to favour outputs from their own model family.
  • Leniency and compression: scores bunch at the top of a 1-5 scale.
  • Rubric sensitivity: small wording changes move scores.

Mitigations. Binary or three-level criteria with explicit definitions and examples; one criterion per call; reasoning before the verdict; a judge at least as capable as the system under test and preferably from a different family; pinned judge version.

Correcting for judge error. If the judge has true positive rate TPR and false positive rate FPR on the labelled set, an observed pass rate \(p_{obs}\) implies a true rate \(\hat p = (p_{obs} - \mathrm{FPR}) / (\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR})\). With TPR 0.9 and FPR 0.2, an observed 76% corresponds to 80%.

Re-validate whenever the judge model, the rubric or the product’s output distribution changes.

  • Judge-human agreement is 85% and human-human is 80%. What does that mean?
  • How does the correction formula behave when TPR is close to FPR?
  • Apple, Machine Learning Engineer, Aug 2025: Annotation agreement, and LLM versus human judges (PracHub)

Pairwise or pointwise judging? And what makes a rubric good?

Pointwise assigns each output an absolute verdict or score. It scales linearly in outputs, gives a level you can threshold and track over time, and suits regression gates and production monitoring. Its weakness is calibration: absolute scores drift between raters and judge versions, and bunch at the top of the scale.

Pairwise asks which of two outputs is better. People and models are more consistent at comparing than at absolute scoring, so it detects smaller differences with fewer examples. Its weaknesses: no absolute level (both can be bad), position bias, intransitive preferences, and quadratic growth in comparisons with many systems, handled by sampling pairs and fitting Elo or Bradley-Terry ratings. Allow ties.

Use pairwise for selecting between two prompts or models; use pointwise pass/fail for gates, monitoring and anything that needs a stable number.

Rubric design.

  • Decompose quality into independent criteria (correct, grounded, complete, follows format) and grade each separately.
  • Prefer binary or three levels with observable definitions. A 1-10 scale has levels nobody can distinguish.
  • Give anchor examples for each level, including borderline cases with the reasoning.
  • Say what to ignore (length, style) if it should not count.
  • Treat critical failures (unsafe, fabricated fact) as separate gates; averaging hides them.
  • Pilot the rubric on 30-50 items with two raters, find where they disagree, and revise the wording until agreement is acceptable.

A rubric that humans cannot apply consistently will not be applied consistently by a model.

  • How many pairwise comparisons would you need to rank five systems?
  • Your judge says A beats B, B beats C and C beats A. What do you do?

How is evaluating an agent different from evaluating a single model response?

An agent produces a trajectory with side effects, is more variable, and costs far more per example.

Outcome versus trajectory grading.

  • Outcome: check the final environment state (tests pass, the record has the right values, the file exists). It accepts any valid path, so prefer it for task success.
  • Trajectory: check the steps (tools used, unnecessary calls, policy violations such as acting without confirmation, efficiency). Use it for diagnosis and for constraints that must hold along the way. Requiring one exact path penalises valid alternatives.

Environments. Sandboxed and resettable with a deterministic start state: containers, seeded databases, mocked or recorded external services. No state may leak between runs. Live dependencies (the web, third-party APIs) make results non-stationary.

Variance. Run each task \(k\) times. Report mean success with a confidence interval, and if reliability matters, the fraction of tasks solved in all \(k\) trials, which is much lower than the mean for unreliable agents. Separate infrastructure failures (timeouts, sandbox errors) from agent failures.

Cost. Record tokens, steps, wall-clock time and money per task; a method that gains two points at three times the cost is a different trade. Tier the suites: a small smoke set per change, the full set nightly.

Grader validity. Confirm that a reference solution passes and a do-nothing agent fails. Read transcripts: agents find shortcuts such as editing the tests, hard-coding expected output or exploiting a lenient check.

Reporting. State the harness, tools, step and token budgets with the score, since the same model scores differently under different scaffolds.

  • A task passes 3 of 5 trials. How do you count it?
  • How do you evaluate an agent whose tasks touch the live web?
  • OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, Apr 2026: Agent harness and evaluation system for a tool-using agent (PracHub)

You upgraded the judge model and quality scores moved by several points overnight with no product change. What do you do?

Confirm the cause. Take a frozen set of stored product outputs and score them with the old and the new judge. Identical outputs with different scores isolate the judge effect from any product change.

Decide which judge is right. Score the human-labelled calibration set with both. Compare agreement with humans, true and false positive rates, and the score distribution. Read the items where the judges disagree, grouped by criterion and slice: the new judge may be stricter on one criterion, more lenient on long answers, or reading the rubric differently.

Repair the time series.

  • The judge version is part of the metric definition. Scores from different judge versions are not comparable and should never share a trend line without a marked break.
  • If the new judge agrees with humans at least as well, adopt it and re-baseline: re-score stored historical outputs with it, or run both judges in parallel for an overlap period and publish the offset.
  • If it agrees worse, stay on the pinned old version and adjust the rubric for the new one before switching.

Prevent recurrence.

  • Pin a dated judge snapshot; never a moving alias.
  • Store raw outputs so they can be re-scored.
  • Run the calibration set through the judge in CI and alert when judge-human agreement or the judge’s pass rate on a fixed reference set moves.
  • Version rubric, judge model and judge prompt together and log them with every score.

The same procedure applies when the rubric is edited, which is a more frequent cause than model upgrades.

  • You did not store historical outputs. What can you still do?
  • The provider retires the old judge model next month. Plan the transition.

What makes a benchmark result untrustworthy? Cover contamination, overfitting and saturation, and say how you would report results properly.

Contamination. Test items, or close paraphrases, were in the training data, so the score measures recall. Public benchmarks are scraped into pretraining corpora. Signs: a large drop on freshly written or post-cutoff items, on rephrased questions, or when answer options are reordered; the model completing a test item verbatim. Mitigations: private held-out sets, periodically refreshed items, and canary strings in published data.

Overfitting to the benchmark. Repeatedly choosing models, prompts and hyperparameters on the same test set selects for noise in that set, even with no leakage. Keep a development split for iteration and look at the test split rarely. Community-wide reuse has the same effect over years.

Saturation. When scores approach the ceiling, remaining differences are within noise and within the label error rate. A benchmark with 3% wrong labels cannot distinguish 96% from 97%.

Construct validity. A benchmark is a sample of some skill. Check that it resembles your task; a leaderboard gain may not transfer.

Reporting.

  • Number of items and a confidence interval for every score.
  • Paired comparison between systems on the same items.
  • Variance across seeds or repeated runs for sampled outputs.
  • The full setup: prompt, few-shot examples, decoding settings, tools, scaffold and budgets. Agent benchmark scores depend heavily on the harness.
  • Cost and latency next to accuracy.
  • Which results were selected after looking at the test set.
  • How would you test a model for contamination on a benchmark you did not create?
  • Your team has tuned on the same test set for a year. What now?

Model B scores 83% and model A 80% on your 500-example eval. Is B better? Show the calculation.

It depends on whether the comparison is paired, and it should be, since both models ran on the same examples.

Unpaired view. The standard error of an accuracy is \(\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}\). The difference has

\[ \mathrm{SE} = \sqrt{\tfrac{0.80 \cdot 0.20}{500} + \tfrac{0.83 \cdot 0.17}{500}} \approx 0.0245, \]

so the 95% interval is \(3 \pm 4.8\) points: not significant.

Paired view. With per-example scores \(a_i, b_i\) and \(d_i = b_i - a_i\),

\[ \mathrm{Var}(\bar d) = \frac{\sigma_A^2 + \sigma_B^2 - 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(a, b)}{n}. \]

Two models tend to get the same examples right, so the covariance is positive and the variance shrinks. For binary scores only discordant examples matter. Suppose A alone is right on \(n_{10} = 10\) and B alone on \(n_{01} = 25\) (difference \(15/500 = 3\) points):

  • McNemar: \(\chi^2 = (n_{01} - n_{10})^2 / (n_{01} + n_{10}) = 225/35 \approx 6.4\), \(p \approx 0.011\).
  • \(\mathrm{SE}(\bar d) = \sqrt{n_{01} + n_{10} - (n_{01} - n_{10})^2/n}\,/\,n \approx 0.0118\), so the interval is \(3 \pm 2.3\) points.

Same data, significant once paired. With 60 and 75 discordant examples instead, the same 3 points would not be.

Caveats.

  • This covers sampling of examples only. If outputs are sampled, add run-to-run variance by repeating runs.
  • Examples that share a source document or user are not independent; use clustered standard errors or a cluster bootstrap.
  • If B is the best of many variants tried on this set, the p-value is optimistic.

Sizing. To detect a difference \(\delta\), the interval half-width must be below \(\delta\); halving the detectable difference needs four times the examples.

  • Why does a paired test need fewer examples?
  • What changes if each example is graded on a 1-5 scale instead of pass/fail?

Implement a bootstrap confidence interval for the difference in a metric between two systems evaluated on the same examples.

import numpy as np

def paired_bootstrap_diff(a, b, n_boot=10_000, alpha=0.05, seed=0, groups=None):
    """a, b: per-example scores of systems A and B on the SAME examples, shape (n,).
    groups: optional cluster id per example (user, document); resample clusters if given."""
    a, b = np.asarray(a, float), np.asarray(b, float)
    assert a.shape == b.shape and a.ndim == 1
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    if groups is None:
        units = [np.array([i]) for i in range(len(a))]
    else:
        groups = np.asarray(groups)
        units = [np.flatnonzero(groups == g) for g in np.unique(groups)]
    diffs = np.empty(n_boot)
    for t in range(n_boot):
        pick = rng.integers(0, len(units), size=len(units))     # resample units with replacement
        idx = np.concatenate([units[j] for j in pick])
        diffs[t] = b[idx].mean() - a[idx].mean()                # same idx for both: paired
    lo, hi = np.quantile(diffs, [alpha / 2, 1 - alpha / 2])
    return {"diff": b.mean() - a.mean(), "ci": (lo, hi), "significant": not (lo <= 0 <= hi)}

Pitfalls an interviewer checks:

  • Pairing. Use the same resampled indices for both systems. Resampling them independently throws away the correlation and widens the interval.
  • Unit of resampling. Resample the independent unit: the conversation, user or source document, not the turn or chunk. Otherwise the interval is too narrow.
  • Metrics that are not means. For corpus-level F1, BLEU or AUC, recompute the metric on each resample; do not average per-example values.
  • Replicates. At least 1,000; 10,000 for stable tails.
  • Small or skewed samples. The percentile interval has poor coverage; use BCa or a permutation test for the p-value.
  • What it does not cover. Only example sampling. For stochastic systems, also resample over repeated runs.
  • Speed. For the simple mean, draw an index matrix of shape (n_boot, n) and vectorise.
  • How would you turn this into a p-value?
  • When does the bootstrap fail outright?

Design the evaluation system for an AI assistant product used by several teams, covering offline evaluation, release gating and production.

Goals. Any change to prompt, model, tools or retrieval gets a trustworthy quality, cost and latency read within minutes to hours; regressions are caught before release; production quality is visible continuously.

Datasets. Versioned and owned.

  • Golden sets per capability and slice, with references or rubrics.
  • A regression set built from past incidents.
  • Safety and adversarial sets.
  • A rolling sample of recent production traffic, privacy-filtered.
  • A held-out set that prompt authors do not see.

Graders. A library of code checks and LLM judges, each with a measured error rate against a human-labelled calibration set, a pinned judge version, and tests. A human review queue for calibration and ambiguous cases.

Runner. Executes a system configuration against a dataset in parallel, with sandboxed tools for agent tasks, multiple trials per case, cached model outputs keyed by configuration, and per-run cost accounting. Every run records the dataset version, grader versions, code commit, model snapshot and prompt version.

Results. A store and UI with per-slice scores and confidence intervals, paired comparison against a baseline, the list of flipped examples, and a link from every score to the trace.

Gates. A smoke suite on every change; the full suite nightly and before release; explicit thresholds for guardrail criteria (safety, format validity, groundedness) and a non-inferiority margin for the primary metric.

Online. The same graders score a sample of production traces; implicit signals (regenerate, edit, abandon, escalate) and A/B tests measure user impact; canary prompts detect upstream model changes.

The loop. Production failures and review-queue findings flow back into datasets; judges are re-calibrated on a schedule.

Trade-offs to state. Suite cost and runtime against coverage, handled by tiering; flaky cases quarantined and fixed, not ignored; one shared platform against team-specific rubrics; and the risk of the suite becoming the target, countered by refreshing it from live traffic.

  • How do you stop teams from tuning to the shared golden set?
  • What is the first thing you would build with two engineers and one month?
  • How do you decide the release threshold for the primary metric?

Which classification metric do you use when positives are rare, and why is accuracy or ROC-AUC not enough?

Definitions: precision \(= TP/(TP+FP)\), recall \(= TP/(TP+FN)\), false positive rate \(= FP/(FP+TN)\). ROC-AUC is the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative. PR-AUC summarises precision over recall.
