As a behavioural story. The competing asks, your criteria, the decision, how you told the people who lost, the result, and what the dropped item actually cost.

Mistakes.

  • Agreeing to all five and slipping all five.
  • “My manager sets priorities.”
  • Choosing the interesting item over the valuable one.
  • No estimates at all.
  • Never revisiting the decision when information changes.
  • How do you estimate impact for work that has never been tried?
  • A senior stakeholder insists their request is urgent. What do you do?

Tell me about a project you stopped. When should you kill your own project?

What is tested. Whether you judge your own work by evidence and not by sunk cost, and whether you can stop in a way that preserves the value and the team.

When to stop. Decide on the future only: continue if the expected remaining value minus the remaining cost beats the best alternative use of the same people. Money and time already spent do not enter. Signals:

  • A ceiling analysis shows a small upper bound: even a perfect version of the component barely moves the end metric.
  • A simpler baseline has caught up.
  • The cost to put it into production exceeds its value (latency, serving cost, maintenance).
  • The premise changed: a new model or API does the job, or the product direction moved.
  • Milestones keep slipping for reasons that are not being resolved.

A strong answer.

  • Kill criteria were set in advance (“if the headroom analysis shows less than X by week 4, we stop”).
  • You proposed stopping, before being asked.
  • You wrote up the negative result with evidence, so nobody repeats it.
  • You salvaged the reusable parts: data, evaluation, tooling.
  • You looked after the team: credit for the work, a clear next assignment.
  • You recorded what would make it worth revisiting.

Mistakes.

  • The project was stopped by someone else and you narrate it as your call.
  • No write-up.
  • Blaming the idea’s originator.
  • Running it months past the evidence.
  • Never having stopped anything.
  • How did you tell the people who had worked on it?
  • How do you tell “not working yet” from “not going to work”?

You launched a model and a key metric regressed. Walk me through the first hour, the first day and the first week.

First hour: contain.

  • Is it real, and is it ours? Check the size against normal noise, the timing against the rollout, and which segments moved.
  • If a guardrail is breached and the link is plausible, roll back or ramp down first. It is cheap and reversible; diagnosis can continue on a small slice or offline.
  • Send one message to stakeholders: what we see, what we did, when the next update comes. They should hear it from you.

First day: diagnose. Work through the causes in order of cost to check:

  • Experiment validity: sample-ratio mismatch, a logging change, an overlapping launch.
  • Training-serving skew: feature parity, preprocessing or tokenizer version, stale or missing features, default values.
  • A latency regression: a slower model lowers engagement by itself.
  • Proxy mismatch: the offline metric improved while the product metric fell (for example clicks up, retention down).
  • Distribution: the offline evaluation set does not represent live traffic; check slices such as new users, locale and platform.

First week: fix the system.

  • A blameless write-up: timeline, impact (quantified), root cause, why it was not caught earlier.
  • Actions with owners: the offline test that would have caught it, a new guardrail, a shadow or canary stage, a parity check.
  • A decision on relaunch, with criteria.

What interviewers listen for. Rollback before debugging, communication without being asked, quantified impact, and a fix to the process as well as to the bug.

Mistakes. Debugging in production while the regression continues; a silent rollback; attributing it to noise without checking; blaming the experiment platform or another team.

  • The offline metric was clearly better. Give three reasons the online metric could still fall.
  • When would you not roll back?

How do you mentor engineers? Give an example of someone you helped grow.

What is tested. Whether you have a deliberate method, whether it adapts to the person, and whether the outcome is theirs.

Structure of the example.

  1. Who: their level and the specific gap (skill, confidence, or context).
  2. What you did:
    • Scoped a task slightly beyond their current level, with a safety net.
    • Agreed what good looks like before they started.
    • Reviewed the design before the code, by asking questions instead of supplying answers.
    • Gave specific and timely feedback: the situation, what they did, its effect. Critical feedback in private.
    • Gave them visibility: they present the result.
    • Withdrew support step by step.
  3. Outcome: what they now do without you (led a project, got promoted, mentors others).

Adapting.

  • New hire: a first merged change in week one, a map of the systems, a named person for questions.
  • Junior: task decomposition, a debugging method, experiment hygiene (one change at a time, a baseline, looking at the data).
  • Peer or senior: sponsorship, and challenge on judgement instead of instruction.
  • Someone struggling: explicit expectations, short feedback cycles, and the manager involved early.

Mistakes.

  • Mentoring described as answering questions.
  • Doing their work for them.
  • Only stories about people who were already strong.
  • No example of difficult feedback.
  • The story is about you.
  • Tell me about feedback you gave that was hard to hear. How did you deliver it?
  • How do you decide when to let someone make a mistake?

What does “raising the bar” mean in practice? What have you done that improved how a whole team works, and not only one person?

What is tested. Leverage: whether your standards outlive your direct involvement.

Mechanisms that work.

  • Review as teaching. Explain the reason, separate blocking issues from preferences, and review the experiment design and the evaluation, not only the code.
  • Standards in tools, not in reminders. Templates for design docs and experiment reports, CI checks, one shared evaluation harness, a rule that every result is reported against a baseline.
  • Shared rituals. A results review where claims are challenged, blameless post-mortems, reading groups tied to current problems.
  • Hiring. Written rubrics, calibrated interviewers, debriefs that weigh evidence.
  • Example. Publishing your own negative results and corrections.

Structure of the story.

  1. A recurring problem you observed (for example, offline gains that did not reproduce).
  2. The cause in the team’s practice.
  3. The smallest mechanism that addresses it.
  4. How you got agreement: a pilot with one team, then results.
  5. Evidence: adoption without your pushing, fewer regressions, faster first contribution from new hires, better documents from others.

Mistakes.

  • Becoming the gatekeeper whom every change must pass.
  • Heavy process on a small team.
  • Standards without a rationale.
  • “Raising the bar” used to mean criticising others.
  • No measure of whether anything changed.
  • Which standard did you introduce that turned out to be wrong or too heavy?
  • How do you raise the bar without slowing the team down?

What goes into a design doc for an ML system, and what makes reviewers trust it?

Sections.

  1. Summary. The recommendation and the decision you need, in a few lines.
  2. Problem and context. Who is affected, why now, the link to a business metric.
  3. Goals and non-goals. Non-goals prevent most scope arguments.
  4. Success metrics. Offline, online and guardrails, with target values.
  5. Current state. The existing system and baseline numbers.
  6. Proposed design. Data (sources, labels, volume, freshness, privacy), model, training, evaluation plan, serving (latency and cost budget, capacity), rollout (shadow, canary, A/B), monitoring, fallback.
  7. Alternatives considered. Include “do nothing” and the simplest non-ML option, each with the reason it was rejected.
  8. Risks and open questions. Including what result would make you stop.
  9. Plan. Milestones with decision points, cost in people and compute, dependencies and requests of other teams.

What earns trust.

  • Numbers with sources, and assumptions stated as assumptions.
  • Honest alternatives, not strawmen.
  • Risks named by the author before a reviewer finds them.
  • Written for a sceptical reader from another team: terms defined, a diagram, no unexplained internal names.
  • Length matched to the decision; two to six pages is typical.
  • Circulated early to the likely critics; decisions and dissent recorded in the doc.

Mistakes.

  • A description of a solution with no problem statement.
  • No metric, or a metric without a target.
  • Written after the system is built, as justification.
  • No explicit request of the reader.
  • Left stale after the design changed.
  • How is a design doc for an ML system different from one for a backend service?
  • A reviewer disagrees with your core choice in the comments. What do you do?

How do you write up an experiment result so that a busy reader reaches the right conclusion?

Put the conclusion first and make every claim checkable.

Structure.

  1. Headline. The conclusion and recommendation in one or two sentences: ship, do not ship, or inconclusive and why.
  2. What was tested. The hypothesis, the single change, the baseline.
  3. Setup. Data or traffic, duration, sample size, metric definitions, and the primary metric chosen in advance.
  4. Results. A table with baseline, treatment, absolute and relative delta, and a confidence interval or seed-to-seed spread. Then guardrails, then the slices where the effect differs.
  5. Interpretation. The likely mechanism, and the alternative explanations you ruled out.
  6. Caveats. Novelty effects, sample-ratio mismatch, multiple comparisons, overlap between evaluation and training data, anything not measured.
  7. Next steps. The decision requested and the follow-up.
  8. Reproducibility. Commit, config, data snapshot, run ids.

Rules.

  • Report null and negative results with the same care.
  • Give both forms of a delta: “+0.4 points (1.2% relative)”.
  • Give intervals and effect sizes, not only “significant”.
  • State the noise floor (an A/A test, or the spread across seeds), so the reader can judge a small gain.
  • One chart per claim, with labelled axes and a visible baseline.
  • Mark slices found after the fact as exploratory.
  • Keep observation (“metric X rose”) separate from inference (“because of Y”).

Mistakes. The conclusion on page three, ten metrics and no primary one, a gain with no baseline, selective slices, and a write-up that cannot be reproduced.

  • The primary metric is flat and one slice shows a large gain. How do you report it?
  • What do you write when the result is inconclusive?

How do you explain a technical decision or a model’s limitation to a non-technical executive or customer?

What is tested. In the interview this is often tested directly: “explain your project to me as if I were in sales”. Signals are structure, absence of jargon, and whether you check understanding.

Approach.

  1. Start from their decision. What do they need to decide or do after hearing you?
  2. Lead with the conclusion and the request.
  3. Use their units: money, time, risk, customers affected. Replace “precision 0.7, recall 0.9” with counts: “of every 100 transactions we flag, about 70 are fraud, and we miss about 1 fraud in 10” (illustrative numbers).
  4. State uncertainty as a range and name what it depends on.
  5. Offer options with their trade-offs and give a recommendation.
  6. For a limitation, cover three things: what it cannot do, what the user sees when it fails, and what the mitigation is.
  7. Check understanding by asking what they will tell their own team, and follow up in writing.

Prepare three depths of the same explanation: 30 seconds, 2 minutes and 10 minutes. Use at most one analogy, and say where it stops being accurate.

Mistakes.

  • Telling the story in chronological order.
  • Hedging every sentence until there is no message.
  • Hiding bad news inside detail.
  • Talking down to the listener.
  • Promising certainty to end the conversation.
  • Explain overfitting to a product manager in three sentences.
  • The executive asks “so is it 95% accurate?” and the honest answer is “it depends on the customer”. What do you say?

Tell me about a time you were given a vague goal, such as “improve search quality” or “do something with LLMs for support”. What did you do first?

What is tested. Whether you create structure yourself. The two failing patterns are waiting for a specification and building the first idea.

A strong sequence.

  1. Find the goal behind the goal. Who owns the outcome, which decision or metric it should move, the constraints, the deadline, what was already tried.
  2. Look at reality. Read 50 to 100 raw examples of failures, check the logs, talk to users or the support team. Size the problem: how often, and at what cost.
  3. Decompose. List the candidate problems and estimate the headroom of each with a quick upper-bound analysis.
  4. Write a one-page framing. Problem statement, metric, hypotheses, first milestone, non-goals. Get agreement on it. This turns ambiguity into something concrete that people can disagree with.
  5. Take the shortest path to learning. A baseline and an evaluation in days. Time-box each exploration with the question it must answer.
  6. Report uncertainty. What is known, what is not, and when the next decision point is.
  7. Re-plan as evidence arrives.

Name the kind of ambiguity, because the action differs: an unclear goal needs a conversation with the owner; an unclear approach needs experiments; unclear ownership needs an explicit agreement on who decides.

Mistakes.

  • Asking the manager for a full specification.
  • A month of building before any measurement.
  • Analysis without a deadline.
  • Nothing written down, so the framing drifts.
  • Describing the ambiguity as someone else’s failure.
  • How did you decide the first thing to measure?
  • How did you know your framing was the right one?

You join as the first ML engineer on a new product. There is no data pipeline, no evaluation and no model. How do you sequence the first 90 days?

Build a thin end-to-end slice first, and build the evaluation before iterating on the model.

Weeks 0 to 2: understand and ship version zero.

  • Learn the product and the user; agree the task and the success metric with product.
  • Find what data exists.
  • Ship the simplest thing that works end to end: a heuristic, or a hosted model behind a prompt.
  • Log inputs, outputs and user actions from the first day. Without logs there is no data to improve on.

Weeks 2 to 4: evaluation.

  • A few hundred labelled examples drawn from real usage, with the important slices.
  • An error taxonomy and baseline numbers.
  • One command that produces the numbers in minutes.

Weeks 4 to 8: iterate on the largest error bucket.

  • Simple methods first: prompt and retrieval changes, a small fine-tune, a gradient-boosted model.
  • Release behind a flag to real users, with a fallback and a latency and cost budget.

Weeks 8 to 12: measure online and plan.

  • A staged rollout or A/B test, monitoring, a feedback loop from users into the evaluation set.
  • Decide what to own next. Moving from a hosted API to your own model is justified by volume and unit cost, latency, privacy or domain quality, not by preference.

Principles.

  • Borrow infrastructure. A feature store, a custom training platform or a cluster is rarely needed in the first quarter.
  • Decide reversible things quickly; slow down for the irreversible ones (data schema, labelling policy, privacy commitments).
  • Take on technical debt deliberately and keep a list.

Mistakes. Starting with model architecture, having no logging, iterating by impression with no evaluation set, and polishing before anyone uses it.

  • What would you deliberately not build in the first quarter?
  • How do you get labels when there are no users yet?

When should you not use ML for a problem?

Do not use it when a cheaper, deterministic solution meets the requirement, or when you cannot tell whether the model works.

Conditions against ML.

  • Rules, a lookup or a query are good enough. They are deterministic, debuggable and nearly free to run.
  • No data, no labels, no feedback signal, and no realistic way to get them.
  • Errors are intolerable and unreviewed. No human check, no fallback, no undo.
  • Exact or explainable behaviour is required, by regulation or contract.
  • It cannot pay back. Roughly, value per decision x number of decisions x expected lift must exceed the cost of building, serving, monitoring and maintaining. Low-volume decisions rarely qualify.
  • The effect cannot be measured, so nobody can tell an improvement from a regression.
  • The bottleneck is elsewhere: the interface, the inventory, the latency.

Costs that are easy to forget. Monitoring, drift, retraining, upstream data dependencies, on-call, and feedback loops between the model and its own training data.

Practice. Start with a heuristic baseline. It becomes the benchmark and later the fallback, and ML has to beat it by a margin the product can feel.

The current version of the same question.

  • Do not use an LLM where a regular expression, a small classifier or plain code works: cost, latency and nondeterminism all get worse.
  • Do not use an agent where a fixed workflow works.
  • Do not fine-tune where a prompt with retrieval is sufficient.

Interviewers credit candidates who propose the simple solution before being asked and who put numbers on the comparison.

  • Give an example where you replaced a model with a rule, or chose not to build one.
  • A stakeholder insists on “AI” for a problem that rules solve. What do you do?

How do you choose the metric for an ML product? Give an example where optimising the obvious metric hurts the product.

Build the chain from the business goal down, and check each link, because each is a proxy for the one above.

  1. Business goal: retention, revenue, tasks completed.
  2. Online product metric: sensitive enough to move within an experiment.
  3. Offline metric: computed on a fixed set; useful only if offline gains have historically predicted online gains.
  4. Training loss: what the optimiser sees.

A good metric is aligned with user value, sensitive, available quickly, hard to game, and defined precisely (unit of analysis, time window, denominator).

Guardrails and counter-metrics. Every target needs the metric that would reveal gaming: latency, cost, complaint or harm rate, diversity, long-term retention, performance on important slices.

Examples of the obvious metric failing.

  • Click-through rate rewards clickbait: clicks rise, satisfaction and return visits fall.
  • Watch time rewards content people regret watching.
  • Deflection rate for a support bot rises when users give up. Pair it with re-contact within 7 days and confirmed resolution.
  • Suggestion acceptance rate for a code assistant rises with short, trivial suggestions. Measure the code that is still there later.
  • Fraud recall at a fixed false-positive rate ignores amounts. Weight by value.
  • An LLM-judge score can reward length.

This is Goodhart’s law: a measure that becomes a target stops measuring.

Process. Write the definition down, read examples from both ends of the metric to confirm it means what you think, declare one primary metric and two to four guardrails before the experiment, and agree the decision rule.

  • Your offline metric improves and the online metric does not. What do you investigate?
  • How do you measure long-term effects in a two-week experiment?

How does the cost of errors change your design? Take a classifier whose false positives and false negatives cost very different amounts.

Threshold from costs. With a calibrated probability \(p\) of the positive class and no cost for correct decisions, act when the expected cost of not acting is larger:

\[p\,C_{FN} > (1-p)\,C_{FP} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p > \frac{C_{FP}}{C_{FP} + C_{FN}}.\]

If a missed fraud costs 100 units and a blocked good customer costs 5, the threshold is \(5/105 \approx 0.048\), far from 0.5. When the cost varies per case (the transaction amount), compare expected costs per case instead of using one threshold. This only works if \(p\) is calibrated.

More than two actions. Allow, ask for extra verification, send to manual review, block. The uncertain band goes to the cheaper intermediate action. Review capacity is a constraint: if reviewers handle 500 cases a day, the operating point is precision in the top 500.

Let the product absorb errors.

  • Suggest instead of acting automatically.
  • Make actions undoable and ask for confirmation before irreversible ones.
  • Show sources or confidence where users can act on them.
  • Provide a fallback path when confidence is low.

Evaluate accordingly. Cost-weighted metrics at the operating point, not AUC; calibration; the slices where the cost concentrates.

Rare catastrophic errors are not handled by averages. Use hard constraints: rules, allowlists, human approval.

Feedback effect. Blocked cases never produce a label, so the training data is biased by past decisions. Keep a small randomly approved sample.

For LLM features. The acceptable error rate depends on reversibility and review: a drafted email that a human edits is cheap to get wrong; an executed refund is not. Set the level of autonomy by error cost.

  • Your probabilities are not calibrated. What changes?
  • How do you estimate the cost of a false positive that annoys a customer?

A stakeholder says “we want to reduce churn with AI”. How do you turn that into an ML problem? Give your general procedure.

  1. Action. What will be done differently with a prediction, by whom, and when? Here: a retention offer, or a call from an account manager. No available action means no project.
  2. Value. The current churn rate, what a point of churn is worth, and what the action costs.
  3. Target. A precise label, unit, horizon and prediction time: “will this active subscriber cancel within 30 days, scored weekly, using data up to the scoring date”. Check that the label is observable and when it arrives.
  4. Is prediction the right formulation? The goal is to reduce churn, not to predict it. The customers worth contacting are the ones the action changes (uplift), not the ones with the highest risk: some will leave anyway, and some are reminded to cancel. Uplift needs data from a randomised intervention, so start with a risk model plus a random holdout that measures the incremental effect.
  5. Data. Which features exist at prediction time, how much history, how many positives. Remove leakage, such as a “cancellation requested” flag.
  6. Metrics. Offline: lift in the top decile, PR-AUC, calibration. Online: retention against the holdout, net of the offer’s cost. Guardrails: margin, complaints.
  7. Constraints. Batch scoring is acceptable; the account team can make 200 calls a week, so precision in the top 200 is the operating point; reasons must be shown to the caller; privacy rules apply.
  8. Baseline. A rule (“no login for 14 days”), then a gradient-boosted model.
  9. Agreement. Success and stop criteria, written down with the stakeholder.

Mistakes. Accepting the framing as given, predicting something nobody can act on, optimising AUC, ignoring the capacity of the intervention, and leakage from post-outcome fields.

  • Why can targeting the highest-risk customers reduce retention?
  • The label arrives 30 days late. How does that affect training and monitoring?

Frame each of these as an ML problem in about two minutes each: “cut support costs with an LLM”, “stop fraud losses”, “make search better”.

Use the same five steps each time: action, formulation, label source and its bias, metric, main trap.

Cut support costs.

  • Action: which contacts are answered automatically, which are drafted for an agent, which are routed.
  • Formulation: intent classification, then a retrieval-grounded answer with the option to abstain and escalate. Agent-assist drafting is the lower-risk first step.
  • Data: past tickets with resolutions, and the knowledge base.
  • Metric: contacts resolved without a human and without re-contact within N days, plus satisfaction and cost per resolved contact. Guardrail: wrong-answer rate on an audited sample.
  • Trap: the most frequent intents often need an action (a refund, an address change), so the limit is tool integration and authorisation, not text quality. The knowledge base sets the ceiling.

Stop fraud losses.

  • Action: allow, challenge, review or block, at transaction time, within a budget of tens of milliseconds.
  • Formulation: cost-sensitive binary classification, with anomaly detection for new patterns.
  • Labels: chargebacks arrive weeks later, exist only for transactions that were allowed, and attackers adapt.
  • Metric: value-weighted recall at a fixed approval rate. The business number is fraud loss plus lost good revenue plus review cost.
  • Trap: a random split leaks across time and across entities. Split by time.

Make search better.

  • First diagnose: sample failed sessions (no click, reformulation, abandonment) and bucket them into recall failure, ranking failure, query understanding, missing inventory, interface.
  • Formulation follows the largest bucket: retrieval or query rewriting, learning to rank, spelling and intent models. Missing inventory is not an ML problem.
  • Metric: offline NDCG@k and recall@k on judged queries; online session success and reformulation rate; latency as a guardrail.
  • Trap: click labels carry position bias, and “better” has no meaning until the success event is defined.
  • For the support case, how would you prove that the cost reduction is real?
  • In the fraud case, how do you get labels for transactions you blocked?

You are embedded with a customer who expects an AI feature in production in six weeks. Their data is messy and their expectations come from a demo. How do you run the engagement?

What is tested. Technical judgement, empathy for the customer, and commercial sense, together.

Discovery (week 1).

  • Who pays, who uses it, which workflow, and what success means in their terms (hours saved, error rate).
  • What “production” means to them: number of users, availability, security review.
  • Collect real examples of inputs and desired outputs. They become the evaluation set.
  • Start access, security and data-privacy requests on the first day; they are usually the critical path.

Reset expectations with evidence. Run the system on 50 of their own examples and show the failure categories. Then agree written acceptance criteria: a metric on an agreed test set and a defined scope (which document types, which languages), not “works well”.

Deliver a thin slice. One workflow, with a human reviewing outputs, working end to end in about two weeks. Iterate weekly against the evaluation set, and show the numbers.

Communicate. A weekly written status: done, numbers, risks, requests. One named counterpart. Answer scope additions with a trade, not a flat refusal.

Feed the product. Keep customer-specific configuration separate from product code. Bring general gaps back to the product team with evidence of frequency and value, and do not fork the product quietly.

Hand over. Monitoring, a feedback channel, a runbook, an evaluation set the customer owns, user training.

Hard moments.

  • They demand accuracy that cannot be reached: design the handling of the remaining errors (a review queue) instead of promising a number.
  • Their data cannot support the use case: say so early, with evidence and options.

Mistakes. Promising to please, disappearing to build for three weeks, treating the customer as an obstacle, and shipping a one-off that nobody can maintain.

  • The customer’s champion asks you to commit to 99% accuracy in writing. What do you say?
  • How do you decide whether a customer request belongs in the product?

A product manager asks when the model will reach the target quality. How do you plan and communicate ML work whose outcome is uncertain?

What is tested. Whether partners can plan around you. The two failing answers are a padded single date and “it is research, so it cannot be estimated”.

Approach.

  • Separate what can be estimated from what cannot. Pipelines, serving and evaluation infrastructure are engineering and get dates. Whether a metric reaches a target is uncertain and gets probabilities and decision points.
  • Plan as time-boxed questions. For example: by week 2 a baseline and an evaluation show the size of the gap; by week 4 a headroom analysis shows whether this approach can close it; at week 8 a go or no-go. Commit to the dates of the decisions, not to the result.
  • Give ranges with the main dependency, update them at each milestone, and report a slip when you learn of it, not at the deadline.
  • Take the research bet off the launch’s critical path. Offer fallbacks: ship the baseline, restrict to high-confidence cases, or keep a human in the loop.
  • Make quality visible. Share examples of failures, not only a number, and define “good enough” together from the cost of errors.
  • Ask about their flexibility. The target, the scope or the date can often move if you explain what each buys.

With researchers. Agree what a hand-off contains (a reproducible checkpoint, the evaluation, inference cost), and bring latency and cost limits in at the start, not after the result.

Mistakes. A confident date for an uncertain outcome, silence until the deadline, promising a metric, and treating the question as an imposition.

  • The week-4 analysis says the target is out of reach. How do you tell the PM?
  • How do you estimate the probability that an approach will work?

Why this company, and why are you leaving your current role?

What is tested. Whether your motivation is specific and durable (will you accept, stay and care), and whether there are warning signs such as bitterness or indifference to the work.

Why this company: three parts, 60 to 90 seconds.

  1. The problem or product, specifically. Something you have used or read (the product’s behaviour, an engineering post, a paper), and an opinion about it.
  2. The fit. What you have done that maps onto what they need now.
  3. The growth. What you want to learn or own that this place is unusually suited for.

Test: if the answer could be given unchanged to a competitor, it is too generic.

Why leaving.

  • Describe what you are moving toward: scope, problem, stage, closeness to research or to users.
  • One sentence on what is missing today, without blame.
  • Keep it true and short. If it was a layoff or a reorganisation, say so plainly.
  • Do not criticise your manager or company, and do not disclose confidential details.

Consistency. The answer must agree with what you say you want in other rounds, with the questions you ask, and with the level you are interviewing for.

At senior level, add what you would want to take on in the first year. It shows you have thought about their problems, not only your career.

Mistakes. Flattery, “looking for a new challenge”, a long career history, complaints, and sounding as if any offer would do.

  • What would make you stay at your current company?
  • What concerns do you have about this role?

What questions do you ask your interviewers, and what do your questions signal?

Questions serve two purposes: information for your own decision, and a signal of level, since they show what you think matters. Prepare two or three per interviewer, and prefer a follow-up to something they said.

Hiring manager.

  • What does success look like in this role at 6 and 12 months?
  • What is the hardest problem the team has now?
  • How are priorities set, and what was deprioritised last?
  • What distinguishes senior from staff here?
  • Why is the role open?

Engineers.

  • How does an idea get from proposal to production, and how long does that take?
  • What do the evaluation and experiment tools look like, and what is painful?
  • How is time split between new work and maintenance? What is on-call like?
  • How does the team use coding agents, and what are the review norms?

Researchers.

  • How is work divided between research and engineering?
  • How is compute allocated?
  • How are research bets chosen and stopped?

Product and other partners.

  • Which metric is the team judged by?
  • How are quality, cost and latency trade-offs decided?

Senior leaders.

  • What is the largest risk to the strategy over two years?

Reading the answers. Warning signs: no clear metric, no evaluation, “we will work out the scope later”, vagueness about why the last person left.

Mistakes.

  • No questions.
  • Questions answered on the careers page.
  • Compensation and logistics put to an engineer; those go to the recruiter.
  • Asking only about promotion.
  • Not listening to the answer.
  • What would an answer have to contain for you to decline the offer?

What do interviewers write down to decide between mid-level, senior and staff? What does the debrief look for?

Interviewers record evidence against rubric dimensions. Names vary by company; the content is similar.

Dimension Senior evidence Staff evidence
Scope and impact Owned a multi-month project end to end with a measured outcome Outcomes across teams or a whole area, repeated over several projects
Technical judgement Explains choices, alternatives and trade-offs; has debugged hard problems Sets architecture and standards; anticipates failure modes; knows when not to build
Ambiguity Turns a vague goal into a plan Decides which problems matter and defines the roadmap
Execution Delivers, unblocks themselves, recovers from setbacks Delivers through others and reduces the risk of large bets
Collaboration and influence Works well with partners; mentors Changes other teams’ direction; develops senior engineers
Communication Clear and structured Writing that drives decisions beyond the team

What ends up in the notes.

  • Specific behaviours: “proposed a baseline first”, “gave a latency budget without being asked”.
  • Whether “I” and “we” were distinguishable.
  • Who drove the design discussion.
  • The reaction to hints and to pushback.
  • Consistency between rounds.

In the debrief.

  • Level follows repeated evidence across rounds, not one strong story.
  • A weak result on a required dimension usually caps the level.
  • The project deep-dive and system design carry most of the levelling weight. Coding is commonly a bar to clear at senior and above, though companies differ.

Preparation. Build a grid of six to eight stories against these dimensions, with at least two stories per dimension, and state the scope explicitly each time: team size, duration, metric.

  • Which dimension is your weakest, and which story covers it?
  • How would your current manager describe the scope of your last project?

What are the most common reasons a candidate for senior or staff is down-levelled, and how do you avoid each?

Past-work rounds.

  • Scope is not shown. The stories are tasks assigned by someone else. Choose stories where you defined the problem, and state the scope.
  • “We” throughout. Your contribution cannot be separated from the team’s.
  • No measured impact. Things were shipped, but nothing is said about what changed. Bring numbers; relative ones if confidential.
  • Shallow depth. Cannot answer “why” two levels down in their own project.
  • Narrowing trajectory. The best work is several years old.

Design rounds.

  • Feature-level design. No requirements, no numbers, no trade-offs, waits to be led.
  • One-sided ML design. All model and no system, or the reverse.
  • Complexity bias. Reaches for the sophisticated architecture before the baseline.
  • One solution presented as obviously correct.

Behavioural rounds.

  • No real conflict, failure or influence story.
  • Blame directed at others.
  • Rambling, or answering a different question.

Coding. Correct but slow, many hints needed, no tests, no complexity analysis. A working but untested solution reads as mid-level.

Specific to staff. Strong individual execution with no evidence of influence beyond the team, no direction-setting and no people developed. The usual outcome is “strong senior”.

Structural factors. Years of experience and current title set the starting assumption, and so does interviewing in a domain you have not worked in.

What to do. Ask the recruiter early which level the loop is calibrated for and what its rubric emphasises. If you are down-levelled, ask which signals were missing; a lower level at a company with a higher bar is not always a worse outcome.

  • Which of these applies most to you, and what have you changed in your preparation?

Ship a simple model now, or a better one in three months? Walk me through how you weigh quality, speed, cost and risk.

Name the variables. The cost of delay per week, the expected quality gain and its uncertainty, the cost to build and to serve, the risk (what breaks, and for how many users), and reversibility.

Default. Ship the simple version behind a flag if it clears the “useful and safe” bar. It starts the feedback and data loop, tests demand, and forces the serving, logging and evaluation path to exist, which the better model needs anyway. Then upgrade.

Exceptions.

  • A poor first version is costly or hard to undo: trust-sensitive features, safety, an enterprise pilot.
  • The simple version creates lock-in or a migration you will pay for later.
  • The simple version does not clear the bar.

Quantify where possible.

  • Expected value: probability of success x gain x traffic x duration, minus cost.
  • Serving cost: if the larger model costs five times more per request, the gain must cover it at your volume.
  • Latency: a quality gain that breaks the latency budget may be a net loss.

Reversibility decides the speed. Reversible decisions are made quickly and cheaply. Irreversible ones (data schema, a public API, privacy commitments, a contract) get more care.

Risk controls buy speed. A canary, a kill switch, a fallback and monitoring make it safe to ship earlier.

Technical debt. Take it on purpose, write it down, and name the trigger for paying it back.

Build or buy. Use a hosted model to move fast. Move to your own or a fine-tuned model when volume makes the unit cost dominant, or when latency, privacy, control or domain quality require it. Work out the break-even.

A senior answer names what would change the decision. Pragmatic does not mean careless.

  • What evidence would make you delay the launch?
  • How do you compute the break-even between a hosted API and self-hosting?

You are asked to set the technical direction of an ML area for the next year. How do you produce a roadmap that people actually follow?

1. Diagnose before proposing.

  • Current state: the metrics, the system, where engineers’ time goes, incidents and post-mortems.
  • Headroom, measured: error breakdowns and ceiling analyses, not opinions.
  • External change: model capability, cost per token or per GPU-hour, new tooling.
  • The business strategy the area must serve.

2. Make choices. A strategy is a diagnosis, a few guiding choices and coherent actions; a list of everything desirable is not one. State what will not be done.

3. Define two to four bets. For each: the hypothesis, the expected impact as a range, the cost, the first milestone and decision point, the kill criteria, the owner. Balance the set: dependable increments, platform investments that speed up everything else (evaluation, data, infrastructure), and one or two high-variance bets.

4. Sequence by dependency and by learning value. Evaluation and data foundations come first; cheap experiments that reduce the risk of the big bets come early.

5. Build agreement. Circulate drafts to the people who must execute and to those who can block. Incorporate objections or record them. Decide in a meeting on a written document, with explicit disagree-and-commit.

6. Operate it. Quarterly milestones, a review cadence, and a version history. In ML the facts change within months, so the roadmap is the current best set of bets and should be revised openly.

Artefacts. A target architecture, standards (how we evaluate, how we ship), and a list of deprecations.

Failure modes.

  • A wish list with no trade-offs.
  • Written alone and announced.
  • Migration cost and team capacity ignored.
  • Re-planning at every new model release.
  • No follow-up after the kickoff.

In an interview, tell it as a case: the diagnosis, what you chose not to do, who disagreed, and what happened.

  • Which bet on your last roadmap failed, and when did you find out?
  • A new model release makes one of your bets obsolete mid-year. What do you do?

What does end-to-end ownership mean for an ML engineer? Give an example of something you did outside your formal remit because the outcome needed it.

Definition. Ownership is accountability for the outcome (the user or business metric), not for the task (a model was trained). For ML it spans the whole chain: problem definition, data, model, evaluation, serving, launch, monitoring, iteration, and retirement.

Behaviours interviewers look for.

  • Notices and closes gaps that fall between teams: a labelling bug, a logging error, a broken dashboard.
  • Stays after launch: watches the metrics, carries the pager, does the post-launch analysis.
  • Raises risks early and says what is not known.
  • Follows a problem to resolution; filing a ticket is not the end.
  • Decides reversible matters within their remit and informs others, and escalates what is irreversible, cross-team or outside their expertise.
  • Cleans up: documentation, dead experiments, unused compute.

Structure of the example.

  1. The gap you noticed.
  2. Why it was nobody’s job.
  3. What you did, including who you informed.
  4. The result.
  5. The systemic fix, so that it does not depend on heroics next time.

The hiring manager’s underlying question is: can I hand this person a problem and not need to check?

Mistakes.

  • A hero story that reveals poor planning.
  • Overriding another team instead of working with them.
  • Ownership described as long hours.
  • Ownership as control: unable to delegate.
  • A list of responsibilities instead of an outcome.
  • Tell me about something you owned that failed after you handed it over.
  • Where is the line between ownership and stepping on another team’s remit?

How do you structure an answer to an ML or AI system design question in a 45-minute round, and where do candidates most often lose it?

One skeleton fits every prompt; what changes is where the depth goes.

Minutes Step What you produce
0-5 Clarify Users, the decision the system makes, scale, latency, constraints, what exists today
5-9 Metrics One online goal metric, offline proxies, guardrails
9-14 High-level design Request path and training path as a box diagram
14-30 Data and labels, Architecture Depth in the two or three places where the risk is
30-36 Serving Latency budget split, capacity arithmetic, cost
36-41 Evaluation and launch Offline gate, shadow, A/B, ramp
41-45 Failure modes and iteration What breaks, monitoring, next steps, a short summary

Habits that carry the round

  • State assumptions as numbers and compute aloud: average QPS is daily requests divided by 86,400, peak is two to three times that; storage is items times bytes; GPU count is peak load divided by measured per-GPU throughput.
  • Start from the simplest baseline that could ship and justify each addition by the failure it fixes.
  • Say where labels come from and what bias they carry before naming a model.
  • Check in at each transition: “I plan to go deep on retrieval; is that where you want depth?”

Common ways to lose it

  • Naming a model architecture in the first two minutes, before the objective is fixed.
  • No numbers, so nothing constrains the design and every choice sounds equally good.
  • Training described in detail, with no serving path, monitoring or launch plan.
  • Offline metrics only, or metrics added at the end.
  • Listing every technique known instead of choosing one and defending it.
  • Missing the interviewer’s hints about where they want depth.
  • Running out of time before evaluation and failure modes.
  • For LLM systems: no evaluation plan, no cost estimate, guardrails that exist only in the prompt.

What a senior answer adds

Prioritisation (what not to build in version one), trade-offs stated with their cost, a degraded mode for every critical dependency, and ownership of the system after launch.

  • The interviewer gives no scale numbers. What do you do?
  • How do you recover when you realise at minute 25 that you went deep on the wrong component?

Design the home-feed recommendation system for a short-video product.

Clarify. Assume 100M daily users, about 40 feed requests per user per day returning 8 videos each, a corpus of 1B videos with 20M uploads per day. That is 4B requests per day: about 46k QPS on average and 120k at peak. Server budget 200 ms at p99. The goal is long-term retention, not clicks.

Metrics. Online: D1/D7 retention, time spent, sessions per user. Guardrails: report and not-interested rates, exposure concentration across creators, impressions for new videos, latency, cost. Offline: recall@K per retrieval source; per-task AUC grouped by user, and calibration.

Data and labels. Impressions are logged with the features served at request time, which removes training-serving skew. Labels: watch time, completion, like, share, follow, comment; negatives: fast skip, not-interested, report. Biases: only shown items get labels, position, and a popularity feedback loop. Watch time must be normalised by duration (for example, quantile within a duration bucket) or long videos win.

Architecture. A funnel of 1B to about 5,000 to 500 to 8.

  • Retrieval from several sources: two-tower ANN trained with in-batch negatives and a sampling-bias correction, item-to-item co-engagement, the follow graph, a fresh-video pool, trending.
  • Pre-rank: a light model distilled from the ranker.
  • Rank: a multi-task model (MMoE or PLE) with target attention over the user’s recent history, one head per engagement; a value score \(\sum_k w_k \hat p_k\) whose weights are tuned online.
  • Re-rank: diversity (MMR or DPP), creator de-duplication, policy filters, exploration slots.
  • Cold start: content-embedding retrieval and a small guaranteed impression budget per new video.

Serving. Budget: retrieval 30 ms, features 20, pre-rank 20, rank 60, re-rank 10, the rest network and margin. Ranking load is 120k x 500 = 60M candidate scorings per second at peak, which is why the pre-rank stage exists and why the ranker runs batched on GPU with cached item-side computation. An embedding table for 1B ids at 64 float32 dimensions is 256 GB, so embeddings live in a sharded parameter service. Models train continuously from the log stream with minutes of delay.

Evaluation and launch. Offline replay, then an A/B test at 1% read over at least two weeks to get past novelty, a long-term holdback, and creator-side analysis because users in different arms share the same content supply.

Failure modes and iteration. Clickbait (engagement up, retention down), filter bubbles, popularity collapse, stale models on a shifting corpus, a model trained only on its own exposure. Mitigate with exploration traffic and propensity-style weighting.

What a senior answer adds. Treats the value function as the product decision, sizes every stage, names the bias each logging choice introduces, and has a degraded mode (serve pre-rank scores when the ranker is overloaded).

  • How do you set the weights in the value function, and who owns that decision?
  • Retention is flat but time spent is up 2%. Do you launch?
  • How would you add a generative or sequence-based retriever to this funnel?
  • OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, Dec 2025: End-to-end recommendation system for a personalised feed (PracHub)
  • Google, Machine Learning Engineer, Aug 2026: Watch-next video recommender, with its losses and optimiser updates derived (PracHub)
  • Google, Machine Learning Engineer, Dec 2025: Real-time recommendation system (PracHub)
  • Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Jul 2026: Large-scale personalised recommendation system end to end (PracHub)
  • Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Feb 2026: Short-video recommendation system (PracHub)

Design search ranking for a large marketplace, including query understanding.

Clarify. Assume 50M daily users and 6 queries each: 300M queries per day, 3.5k QPS on average, about 10k at peak. 500M listings. Queries are short (two to four words) with a long tail. Budget 300 ms at p99.

Metrics. Online: conversion or long-click rate per search, reformulation rate, zero-result rate, abandonment. Offline: NDCG@10 on graded human judgments, recall@1000 for retrieval, all split by head, torso and tail. Guardrails: latency, seller-side exposure, revenue.

Data and labels. Click and purchase logs carry position bias; correct with propensities estimated from small randomised swaps, or a click model. Graded relevance judgments from trained raters anchor NDCG, optionally extended by LLM labelling that is audited against raters. Hard negatives are items shown high and skipped.

Architecture.

  • Query understanding: normalise, spell-correct, classify category and intent, extract attributes (brand, colour, size), generate rewrites or expansions, embed the query. Extracted attributes become boosts unless confidence is high; a wrong hard filter gives zero results. Results for head queries are cached.
  • Retrieval: BM25 on an inverted index with structured filters, dense ANN from a two-tower model, and query-to-item co-click recall; the union is about 10k candidates. Rewrites add recall paths and do not replace the original query.
  • L1: a cheap scorer cuts to 500.
  • L2: LambdaMART or a neural ranker over text-match, behavioural, price, quality and personalisation features.
  • L3: a distilled cross-encoder re-scores the top 50.
  • Final layer: diversity, sponsored blending, policy.

Serving. Budget: query understanding 30 ms, retrieval 50, L1 20, features 30, L2 50, cross-encoder 60, margin 60. The cross-encoder sees 10k x 50 = 500k query-item pairs per second at peak. At an assumed 5k pairs per second per GPU that is 100 GPUs, so score only queries where L2 is uncertain, and cache scores for head queries.

Evaluation and launch. Offline NDCG as a gate, then interleaving, which detects ranking differences with much less traffic than an A/B test, then an A/B test on conversion read by query segment.

Failure modes and iteration. Over-confident attribute filters, rewrites that drift from the intent, position-bias feedback loops, cold-start listings, seasonality, sellers stuffing keywords. Monitor zero-result and reformulation rates per segment and mine reformulation pairs as training data for rewriting.

What a senior answer adds. Checks the retrieval ceiling before investing in ranking (if the relevant item is not in the 10k, no ranker helps), decides which query-understanding outputs are constraints and which are features, and reports every metric by head and tail.

  • How do you estimate position bias without hurting users?
  • Tail queries have almost no click data. How do you rank them?
  • Where would you put an LLM in this system, and what would it cost?

Design click-through-rate prediction and the auction for feed ads.

Clarify. Assume 1B ad requests per day: 12k QPS on average and 35k at peak. 10M active ads. The ad decision has about 100 ms inside the page request. Advertisers bid per click or optimise for conversions.

Metrics. Business: revenue per thousand impressions, advertiser value (conversions, return on spend), user cost (ad hides, organic engagement). Model: log loss or normalised entropy, and calibration (predicted over observed) by slice. AUC is secondary, because the auction uses the probability value and not only the order.

Data and labels. Impressions with click labels; conversions arrive hours to days later inside an attribution window, so use a waiting window plus a correction, or model the delay. Negatives are downsampled at rate \(s\) and predictions corrected by \(\operatorname{logit}(p)=\operatorname{logit}(p_s)+\log s\). Only auction winners get labels, so reserve exploration traffic.

Architecture.

  • Candidate selection: targeting index plus embedding retrieval, 10M to about 2,000.
  • A light model cuts to 200.
  • Heavy model: id embeddings, feature crosses, user behaviour sequence; multi-task pCTR and pCVR, trained on the whole impression space to limit CVR selection bias; then a calibration layer.
  • Auction: rank by \(\text{eCPM}=1000\cdot b\cdot\hat p_{\text{CTR}}\) for click bids, or \(1000\cdot b_{\text{conv}}\cdot\hat p_{\text{CTR}}\cdot\hat p_{\text{CVR}}\) for conversion bids. With generalised second pricing the winner pays per click \(b_2\hat p_2/\hat p_1\), the lowest bid that keeps its slot. Add reserve prices, a quality term and budget pacing.

Calibration matters because the prediction multiplies a bid: a 10% over-prediction over-ranks the ad and, for conversion bidding, overcharges the advertiser by 10%.

Serving. 35k x 200 = 7M heavy scorings per second at peak. Budget: selection 15 ms, features 15, light model 10, heavy model 30, auction 5. Train continuously on the event stream; published results show measurable loss from stale models (He et al., 2014, report roughly 1% in normalised entropy between weekly and daily retraining).

Evaluation and launch. Offline on a later time slice, never a random split. Online, both arms draw on the same advertiser budgets, which biases a naive A/B test, so use budget-split experiments. Read revenue, advertiser value and user cost together.

Failure modes and iteration. Miscalibration on new ads (use priors and an exploration bonus), feedback loops, click fraud, delayed conversions making new campaigns look worse than they are, advertisers changing bids in response to a launch.

What a senior answer adds. Incentives (second pricing is not truthful in multi-slot auctions; VCG is), per-slice calibration monitoring, marketplace-level experiment design, and long-term advertiser and user value over short-term revenue.

  • Why does a model with better AUC sometimes lose revenue?
  • How do you handle conversions that arrive seven days after the click?
  • What changes when advertisers use automated bidding?
  • Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Jan 2026: Low-latency ads ranking with calibration (PracHub)
  • Meta, Data Scientist, Oct 2025: Ad recommendation and ranking system (PracHub)
  • TikTok, Data Scientist, Oct 2025: Ad selection across three advertiser objectives (PracHub)

Design LLM-based query rewriting inside a search engine where the rewrite must fit a tight latency budget.

Clarify. Assume 20k QPS at peak and a 300 ms p99 search budget, of which rewriting may use 50 ms, in parallel with other query processing. The rewrite should improve recall and relevance for queries that fail (ambiguous, misspelt, vocabulary mismatch) and do nothing for queries that already work.

Metrics. Online: click or long-click rate, reformulation rate, zero-result and low-result rates. Guardrails: intent drift (share of rewrites that change the meaning, from side-by-side judgments), harm rate on queries that were already good, p99 latency, GPU cost per thousand queries. Offline: retrieval gain from the rewrite on held-out queries, judged result quality for original versus rewritten.

Data and labels. Sources: user reformulation chains ending in a click (query, later successful query), a large teacher LLM generating candidates, and filtering of both by measured retrieval improvement and a judge. Reformulation logs include topic changes, so filtering is required.

Architecture. Three tiers.

  1. Precomputed: head and torso queries are rewritten offline or nearline by the large model and stored by normalised query. Assume this covers 60% of volume.
  2. Gate: a cheap classifier decides whether a tail query needs rewriting; assume it passes 30% of the remaining 8k QPS, about 2.4k QPS.
  3. Online student: a small model (under about 1B parameters) distilled from the teacher by supervised fine-tuning, then tuned with a reward from search-result quality.

The rewrite is an extra recall path merged with the original query’s results, which bounds the damage of a bad rewrite.

Serving. Output is about 10 tokens. With an assumed 10 ms prefill and 3 ms per token, generation takes about 40 ms; measure this on the target hardware. Cap output tokens, use a short fixed prompt with a cached prefix, and decode greedily. At an assumed 150 requests per second per GPU within the latency target, 2.4k QPS needs 16 GPUs, about 25 with headroom. A hard timeout falls back to the original query.

Evaluation and launch. Offline gate on retrieval gain and drift rate; shadow traffic for latency; A/B with the harm guardrail; segment by head and tail and by whether a rewrite fired.

Failure modes and iteration. Drift on entities and new terms the model has not seen, over-specific rewrites, reward hacking in the tuning stage (rewriting toward popular queries), cache staleness, a feedback loop when training on logs that the rewriter influenced.

What a senior answer adds. Most of the gain per unit of cost comes from the cache and the gate, not the model; firing rate and quality per fired rewrite are reported separately; personalised rewriting breaks the cache and must justify its cost.

  • How do you decide the gate’s operating point?
  • The rewrite model improves offline retrieval metrics but the A/B test is flat. Why?
  • How would you make rewriting personalised without losing the cache entirely?

Design an enterprise assistant that answers questions over company documents, where each document has access permissions.

Clarify. Assume 50k employees, 20M documents across wikis, drives, tickets and chat, with source-system permissions by user and group. 20 questions per user per day is 1M per day: about 12 QPS on average, perhaps 100 at peak. Load is small; the hard parts are permissions, freshness and answer quality.

Metrics. Answer correctness and groundedness on a labelled set, citation precision, retrieval recall@k, abstention quality (declines when the answer is absent). Online: thumbs, follow-up rate, citation clicks. Hard guardrail: zero permission leaks.

Data and labels. Connectors ingest content, metadata and access-control lists through change feeds, including deletions. A golden set per department: questions, reference answers and source documents, written with domain owners, plus questions with no answer in the corpus.

Architecture.

  • Ingestion: parse by document structure, chunk with headings attached, embed; store text, vector, source, timestamp and allowed principals per chunk.
  • Permissions: resolve the user’s principals (user id plus groups) at query time and filter inside retrieval, so that unauthorised chunks never reach the model. The model is never trusted to withhold. Re-check the top results against the source system before generation, which covers revocations not yet synced.
  • Retrieval: hybrid BM25 and dense, filtered, then a cross-encoder reranker on the top 100, keeping 8 to 10 chunks.
  • Generation: answer only from the supplied context, cite per claim, abstain when support is missing.

Serving. 20M documents at 10 chunks each is 200M chunks; at 1,024 float32 dimensions that is about 820 GB raw, about 205 GB with int8 quantisation. Highly selective filters hurt filtered ANN recall, so use exact search over small permitted subsets or partition by space. Latency: retrieval 100 ms, rerank 150 ms, then streaming with a first token in about a second. Cost: 6k context tokens x 1M queries is 6B input tokens per day, so the context budget is the main cost lever.

Evaluation and launch. Run the golden set on every change to chunking, retrieval, prompt or model. Permission tests with canary documents visible to one test user only. Pilot by department.

Failure modes and iteration. Stale permissions, stale or duplicated documents contradicting each other, prompt injection inside documents (treat retrieved text as data, and limit tools), questions needing aggregation over many documents, tables and scans parsed badly. Use retrieval-miss analysis to choose the next fix.

What a senior answer adds. Permission enforcement as a system invariant with tests, separation of retrieval failures from generation failures in evaluation, a freshness target per connector, and audit logging of what was retrieved for whom.

  • A user is in 2,000 groups. How do you filter efficiently?
  • How quickly must a permission revocation take effect, and how do you guarantee it?
  • The answer is right but cites the wrong document. How do you measure and fix that?
  • OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, Sep 2026: Multi-tenant enterprise RAG assistant with hybrid retrieval, reranking and access controls (PracHub)
  • OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, Aug 2025: End-to-end enterprise RAG search (PracHub)
  • OpenAI, Software Engineer, Dec 2025: Enterprise assistant over internal documents (PracHub)

Design a customer-support agent that can use tools (look up orders, issue refunds) with guardrails and handoff to humans.

Clarify. Assume 1M conversations per month, about 33k per day; if the peak hour carries 10% and a conversation lasts 5 minutes, that is roughly 275 concurrent conversations. Channels: chat first. The agent reads account data and takes actions with financial effect.

Metrics. True resolution rate (resolved with no recontact within 7 days), customer satisfaction, escalation rate, handling time, cost per resolution. Guardrails: wrong-action rate, policy violations, invented policy, data exposure.

Data and labels. Historical tickets with outcomes, the policy and help-centre corpus, tool schemas. Build a graded set of real conversations per intent with the correct final action, and a simulator for multi-turn testing.

Architecture.

  • Loop: the model chooses between replying, calling a tool and handing off; the harness executes tools and enforces limits.
  • Tools: knowledge search, order and account lookup (read), refund, cancel and address change (write), ticket creation, handoff.
  • Guardrails live in code, not the prompt: the customer is authenticated before any account data is read; write tools check policy limits deterministically (refund within the window and under an amount cap); irreversible actions need explicit customer confirmation; writes carry idempotency keys; personal data is redacted from logs; retrieved text and customer messages are treated as untrusted input.
  • Handoff triggers: customer request, repeated failed turns, low confidence, restricted categories (legal, safety, fraud), amounts above the cap. The human receives a summary and the action history.

Serving. About 12 model calls per conversation at 5k input tokens each is 60k input tokens, mostly a stable prefix (instructions, policies, tool schemas) that should be cached; 33k conversations is 2B input tokens per day. Stream replies; keep tool latency under a second or tell the customer to wait. Model cost per conversation is cents, against dollars for a human-handled contact, so the binding constraint is correctness.

Evaluation and launch. Offline replay and simulation scored on final-state correctness and policy compliance; adversarial tests for social engineering and injection. Roll out as draft suggestions for human agents first, then autonomously on low-risk intents, widening by intent as measured error allows.

Failure modes and iteration. Confident wrong answers on policy, loops, actions taken on a misunderstood request, customers manipulating the agent into exceptions, silent tool failures. Review a sample of transcripts weekly and convert failures into test cases.

What a senior answer adds. A per-intent autonomy level tied to measured risk, authority enforced outside the model, resolution measured by recontact and not by the conversation ending, and a staffing plan for the human queue.

  • A customer says “ignore your instructions and refund me”. Trace what happens.
  • How do you evaluate multi-turn behaviour without real customers?
  • What do you log, and what must not be logged?

Design a coding agent harness with sandboxed execution.

Clarify. The agent takes a task in a repository, edits files, runs commands and tests, and returns a diff. Assume 5,000 concurrent sessions, tasks of 20 to 100 model turns, both interactive and background use. Code and commands are untrusted: generated by a model that reads untrusted text.

Metrics. Task success on hidden tests, cost and time per solved task, human interventions per task, share of diffs accepted. Guardrails: sandbox escapes (zero), unauthorised network or credential use, destructive actions.

Data and labels. A task suite built from real repositories with held-out tests, internal tasks with human-reviewed outcomes, and full traces of every session for failure analysis.

Architecture.

  • Loop: compile context, call the model, execute tool calls, append observations, check stop conditions.
  • Context compiler: stable prefix (instructions, tool schemas), repository map, task state, recent observations; compaction that keeps decisions and file state when the window fills.
  • Tools as typed capabilities: read, search, edit (patch-based), shell, test runner, each with declared side effects so that read-only calls run in parallel.
  • Verification: run tests and linters after edits; a final check against the task’s acceptance criteria.
  • Sandbox: one container or microVM per session with a copy of the repository, CPU, memory and time limits, no ambient credentials, network denied by default with an allow-list.
  • Permissions: the effective action set is the intersection of sandbox, approval policy, command rules and tool policy. Risky actions return to a human. The agent cannot change its own permissions.

Serving. 5,000 sessions at 2 vCPU and 4 GB is 10k vCPU and 20 TB of memory if always resident; sessions mostly wait on the model, so snapshot and pause idle sandboxes. A 40-turn task whose context averages 40k tokens reads 1.6M input tokens, so keep the prefix stable to hit the prompt cache, and truncate long tool outputs.

Evaluation and launch. Run the suite on every harness or model change, with several samples per task because outcomes vary. Track success against cost. Release to internal users, then by repository risk level.

Failure modes and iteration. Loops, editing tests to make them pass, destructive commands, prompt injection from repository files or fetched pages, context loss after compaction, flaky tests misread as failures. Each recurring failure becomes a suite task or a harness rule.

What a senior answer adds. Invariants in code and judgment in the model; naming exactly which capabilities sit inside which boundary (external tools may not be sandboxed); cache-aware context design; adding harness structure only for measured failures.

  • The agent needs to install a package from the internet. How do you allow it safely?
  • How do you detect that the agent passed the tests by weakening them?
  • What state must survive a crash so that a session can resume?
  • OpenAI, Machine Learning Engineer, Apr 2026: Agent harness and evaluation system for a tool-using agent (PracHub)
  • Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Jun 2026: LLM-based coding assistant end to end (PracHub)

Design an evaluation platform for LLM products used by many teams.

Clarify. Teams ship prompts, retrieval pipelines, agents and model upgrades. They need to know, before and after release, whether a change is better. Assume 30 teams, suites of about 2,000 cases, and hundreds of evaluation runs per day.

Metrics. For the platform: time from change to trusted result, share of releases gated by an evaluation, agreement between automated graders and humans, agreement between offline results and online outcomes, cost per run.

Data and labels. Versioned datasets with provenance: curated cases, sampled production traces (with privacy filtering), adversarial cases, and regression cases added from incidents. Human labels with a rubric and measured inter-rater agreement. A held-out split per suite that developers do not iterate on.

Architecture.

  • Evaluation as code: a suite declares dataset version, system under test, graders and aggregation.
  • Runner: parallel, rate-limited, resumable, with response caching keyed by model, prompt and parameters.
  • Graders: exact and programmatic checks first; LLM judges with a rubric for open-ended output, each validated against human labels before use and re-validated when the judge model changes; human review queues for samples and disagreements.
  • Agent evaluation: scoring of final state in a sandboxed environment, plus trajectory checks.
  • Results store and reports: scores with confidence intervals, per-slice tables, diffs of individual cases between two runs.
  • Gates: CI blocks a release on a significant regression in a required suite.
  • Online: sample production traces, run the same graders, alert on drift.

Serving. Statistics determine the size. With \(n=2{,}000\) and a pass rate of 0.8 the standard error is \(\sqrt{0.8\cdot0.2/2000}\approx0.9\) points, so two independent runs must differ by about 2.5 points to be distinguishable; paired comparison on the same cases (a paired bootstrap or McNemar’s test) resolves much smaller differences. Cost: 2,000 cases x 3 samples x 20 configurations is 120k generations per day per team before judging, so caching and a small smoke subset matter.

Evaluation and launch. Evaluate the evaluators: judge-human agreement per suite, and whether offline wins predict online wins on past launches. Start with two or three teams and their real release decisions.

Failure modes and iteration. Judges that prefer longer or same-family outputs, suites overfitted by repeated iteration, contamination of public benchmarks, stale datasets after the product changes, nondeterminism read as regression, gates so noisy that teams bypass them.

What a senior answer adds. Graders treated as models with their own validation, every number reported with uncertainty, an explicit link from offline suites to online metrics, and dataset maintenance treated as ongoing work with an owner.

  • How do you validate an LLM judge, and what agreement level is enough?
  • A team’s change shows +1.2 points. Is it real?
  • How do you stop a suite from being overfitted over six months of use?

Design a multi-tenant LLM inference platform serving several models to internal and external customers.

Clarify. Assume 2,000 requests per second at peak, 1,500 prompt tokens and 300 output tokens on average, a handful of base models plus tenant fine-tunes, interactive and batch traffic. Targets: time to first token under 500 ms at p95, steady streaming speed, 99.9% availability.

Metrics. Time to first token, tokens per second per stream, error and rejection rates per tenant, GPU utilisation, cost per million tokens, fairness between tenants under overload.

Data and labels. Traces of request sizes and arrival patterns per tenant drive capacity planning and load tests. Quality evaluations gate every engine, quantisation or model change.

Architecture.

  • Gateway: authentication, quotas and rate limits in tokens per minute, request validation, usage metering.
  • Router: sends requests to a replica that already holds the prompt prefix in cache (session or prefix affinity); spills over when queues grow.
  • Scheduler in each replica: continuous batching, priority classes (interactive above batch), per-tenant fair queueing, admission control on queued tokens.
  • Engine: paged KV cache, prefix caching, quantised weights where evaluations allow, LoRA adapters loaded on a shared base model for tenant fine-tunes.
  • Control plane: model registry, placement, autoscaling on queue time and tokens in flight (GPU utilisation is a poor signal), warm pools because loading 100+ GB of weights takes minutes.

Serving. Demand is 2,000 x 300 = 600k output tokens per second. At an assumed 2,000 output tokens per second per 4-GPU replica of a 70B-class model within the latency target, that is 300 replicas, 1,200 GPUs, about 1,600 with 30% headroom; the per-replica figure must come from load tests. Memory bounds concurrency: with 80 layers and 8 KV heads of dimension 128 in fp16, the cache is \(2\cdot80\cdot8\cdot128\cdot2\) bytes, about 0.33 MB per token, or 2.6 GB for an 8k context. Weights take 140 GB of a 320 GB replica, leaving room for roughly 55 full 8k contexts.

Evaluation and launch. Load tests replaying real traces; canary each engine or model version with automatic rollback on latency or quality regressions; shadow traffic for new quantisation.

Failure modes and iteration. One tenant’s long prompts starving others, retry storms after a brownout (return 429 with retry-after, shed batch load first), cache-affinity hot spots, slow cold starts during a spike, GPU failures, regional outage. Offer a cheaper batch tier to fill off-peak capacity.

What a senior answer adds. Capacity planning in tokens and KV memory rather than requests; isolation and fairness as first-class requirements; cost attribution per tenant; a degradation ladder (shed batch, shorten maximum output, route to a smaller model); and multi-region failover with headroom planned for it.

  • Why is autoscaling on GPU utilisation misleading for LLM serving?
  • How do you serve 500 tenant fine-tunes without 500 deployments?
  • A tenant sends 100k-token prompts. What breaks, and how do you contain it?

Design a fine-tuning and post-training pipeline for a domain model, supervised fine-tuning followed by RL or preference tuning, with evaluation gates.

Clarify. A base model must reach a quality bar on a domain task (assume structured generation with a checkable outcome), at a fixed serving budget, with releases every few weeks. The pipeline must be repeatable by someone who did not build it.

Metrics. A primary task metric from held-out data, an independent quality measure that is not the training reward (human or a separate judge), general-capability and safety regression suites, and behaviour drift from the previous release. Launch criteria are written before training.

Data and labels. Supervised set from curated demonstrations and filtered teacher outputs: deduplicated, split by source and time to prevent leakage, with a manifest of versions and filters. For RL: a prompt set covering the deployment distribution, and a reward. Reward preference order: verifiable outcomes (tests pass, exact match, measured downstream effect), then a learned reward model, then an LLM judge. Preference pairs for DPO come from human or outcome comparisons.

Architecture.

  1. Supervised fine-tuning (full or LoRA), with checkpoint selection on validation.
  2. Gate 1: task metric at or above the incumbent; no regression on general and safety suites; output format valid.
  3. Policy-gradient RL (PPO or GRPO style) or DPO from the gate-1 checkpoint, with a KL or reference-policy constraint, low learning rate, and frequent checkpoints.
  4. Gate 2: reward improves on held-out prompts and the independent measure improves too; drift is bounded; a reward-hacking audit of high-reward samples by reading them.
  5. Registry entry with lineage (data, config, code, parent checkpoint), then shadow and A/B.

Serving. Supervised stage: 200k examples x 1k tokens x 3 epochs is 600M tokens; at an assumed 4k tokens per second per GPU that is about 42 GPU-hours. RL is dominated by rollouts and reward: 2,000 steps x 256 prompts x 8 samples is 4.1M rollouts and 1.2B generated tokens; if a reward call takes 2 seconds, that is about 2,300 hours of reward compute, so it needs around 100-way parallelism to finish in a day. Reward throughput and reliability are designed first.

Evaluation and launch. Compare candidates on the same frozen benchmark, with intervals. Online A/B decides. Keep the incumbent deployable for rollback.

Failure modes and iteration. Reward hacking (length, format tricks, exploiting judge preferences), collapse of output diversity, forgetting of general ability, gains that come from changing how often the model acts and not how well, a reward service outage that corrupts a run, overfitting the benchmark across many checkpoints.

What a senior answer adds. Independence between the training reward and the release metric; gates defined before training; a decomposition of gains into behaviour-rate and per-decision quality; and provenance complete enough to rebuild any released checkpoint.

  • Reward goes up for 1,000 steps while the independent metric falls. What do you do?
  • When would you choose DPO over policy-gradient RL here?
  • How do you choose which RL checkpoint to ship?
  • Meta, Machine Learning Engineer, Sep 2025: Asynchronous RLHF-style post-training system for a production chat model (PracHub)

Design embedding retrieval over a billion items for semantic search.

Clarify. 1B items, 768-dimensional embeddings, 5k QPS at peak, top 100 results in 50 ms at p99, 10M inserts or updates per day, metadata filters on some queries.

Metrics. ANN recall@100 against exact search on a sample, end-to-end recall against labelled relevance, p50 and p99 latency, cost per query, index freshness (time from write to searchable).

Data and labels. Query-item relevance from clicks and judgments to train and evaluate the encoder; a fixed sample of queries with exact nearest neighbours to measure index recall separately from model quality.

Architecture. Memory decides the index type.

  • Raw vectors: 1B x 768 x 4 bytes is 3.07 TB. An in-memory HNSW graph adds links (with degree 32, about 256 bytes per vector at the base layer, another 256 GB), so more than 3.3 TB of RAM across the fleet per replica.
  • IVF with product quantisation: 64-byte codes take 64 GB plus ids. With about 1M inverted lists and 64 probes, a query scans about 64k codes. Recall is lower, so re-score the top 1,000 with full-precision vectors read from SSD.
  • Graph index on SSD with compressed vectors in memory is the third option, with similar re-scoring.

I would choose compressed vectors in memory with full-precision re-scoring, sharded into 20 shards of 50M, each replicated three times, queried by scatter-gather with a merge of the top results.

  • Filters: push selective filters into the index (per-partition indexes or filtered search), and fall back to exact search over the subset when the filter matches few items.
  • Freshness: a small in-memory index for recent writes, merged periodically; deletions by tombstone.

Serving. p99 of a fan-out is governed by the slowest shard, so use hedged requests and per-shard timeouts with partial results. Re-embedding after an encoder upgrade: at an assumed 2,000 items per second per GPU, 1B items take about 140 GPU-hours; build the new index beside the old one and switch atomically, because query and item vectors from different encoder versions are not comparable.
